next_verification: Check WFTU congress minutes, SOBSI leadership lists and the original language used in organizational publications.

atomic_claim_or_observation: TAPOL reported that Ruslan had fought Dutch forces after the 1945 independence proclamation, commanded Pesindo troops, and entered SOBSI leadership after the transfer of sovereignty.
confidence: High that TAPOL reports these details; medium for exact unit and command title
basis_and_limitations: No military service file or Pesindo roster was consulted.
next_verification: Find Pesindo rosters, veteran registration, SOBSI files and family records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: TAPOL and Amnesty report Munir's South Blitar arrest/prison entry as 14 July 1968, while Hearman's reconstruction dates his capture to 13 July; the one-day discrepancy remains unresolved.
confidence: High that the sources give these dates; no confidence in choosing one
basis_and_limitations: Arrest, capture, registration or transfer may be dated differently; no arrest register or contemporaneous family notice was found.
next_verification: Obtain military/police arrest registers, prison intake record, trial file, detention transfer papers and family correspondence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Amnesty reported that Ismail Bakri was arrested in June 1967, sentenced in September 1973, had his life sentence commuted in 1978 to 20 years from arrest, and was released in August 1983.
confidence: High that Amnesty's 1984 annual report gives this chronology; medium pending prison and court records
basis_and_limitations: The report is Amnesty's human-rights summary and its prisoner-of-conscience classification, not the judgment or prison file.
next_verification: Locate the original sentence, commutation decree, remission calculation, prison register and release record.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Amnesty reported that Munir received a death sentence on 12 April 1973, confirmed by the High Court on 23 November 1981 and Supreme Court on 28 March 1983, with presidential clemency rejected in October 1984.
confidence: High that the July 1985 report gives these dates; medium pending original judgments and clemency documents
basis_and_limitations: Amnesty cites reports and case information; the underlying decisions and clemency file have not been inspected.
next_verification: Retrieve trial, high-court and Supreme Court decisions, execution authorization, clemency petition and presidential decision.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Amnesty's May 1985 urgent action and the UN Special Rapporteur's report repeat 14 May 1985 as Munir's execution date, while Amnesty's fuller July 1985 report gives 15 May.
confidence: High that the documents report both dates; unresolved as to the actual execution date
basis_and_limitations: The UN report repeats information provided to it; Amnesty's July report is later and fuller but still not an execution register. Amnesty's August follow-up also repeats 14 May.
next_verification: Locate the execution order, firing-squad/post-operation log, body handover record, family burial and death registration.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Amnesty's May urgent action said Munir's wife was not granted permission to visit before execution, but its July report says he met his wife and family for about three hours on 14 May.
confidence: High that Amnesty reports both; medium for the visit itself pending family testimony
basis_and_limitations: The May text allows that nearby relatives visited; the July text reports a later family meeting. The difference may reflect a changed permission decision or corrected early information.
next_verification: Seek family letters, prison visitor logs, execution notification, photographs and interviews with relatives.

atomic_claim_or_observation: TAPOL reported that Len Murray of the British TUC cabled Suharto on 1 September 1982 to oppose executing Munir and Ruslan, and that Terry Duffy also appealed to Suharto and Kopkamtib head Sudomo.
confidence: High that TAPOL published this account and cable text; medium for transmission/receipt absent cable records
basis_and_limitations: This is post-1965 labor advocacy concerning death sentences, not evidence of covert foreign intervention in the 1965 events.
next_verification: Find the TUC cable and AUEW correspondence, Indonesian presidential and Kopkamtib registries, and replies.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Amnesty reported that after Munir's execution Dutch, Australian and European Community officials appealed against further executions, and that Dutch minister Eegje Schoo met Suharto and the Justice Minister on 25 May 1985.
confidence: High that Amnesty reported these contacts and appeals; medium for individual communications pending government archives
basis_and_limitations: Amnesty summarizes diplomatic reports; Dutch, Australian, Indonesian and European Community files were not directly inspected.
next_verification: Retrieve Dutch foreign-ministry notes, ambassador cables, Schoo's meeting record, Australian diplomatic files and EC appeal text.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A UN Special Rapporteur report reproduced the Indonesian mission's 22 July 1985 statement that Munir's sentence and execution followed normal legal proceedings and due process.
claim_type: Government position reproduced in UN report
confidence: High that the UN report reproduces the government's statement; this is not independent proof of due process
basis_and_limitations: The UN report also records allegations about trial fairness; the government release is an official position, not a judicial re-evaluation or independent finding.
next_verification: Obtain the government's original press release, trial transcripts, counsel access records and appellate judgments.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Amnesty's 1990 report lists Ruslan as tried in a Special Military Court but says in its narrative that the Central Jakarta Subversion Court sentenced him on 15 July 1974.
confidence: High that one Amnesty report gives both court labels; no confidence in choosing one
basis_and_limitations: The underlying judgment and court register have not been located; do not treat the table or narrative as a verified court caption.
next_verification: Retrieve the trial judgment and court docket, appeal records and sentence warrant.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Amnesty listed Ruslan as age 70 in February 1990 and age 77 in its 1995 briefing; TAPOL had described him as about 65 in 1982.
confidence: High that the publications give these approximate ages; no exact birth date established
basis_and_limitations: The figures may be estimates or rounding, and do not support a precise birth year.
next_verification: Seek civil registration, identity papers, family records, school/military records and prison intake files.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Amnesty's 1995 trade-union report calls Ruslan a former ILO 'Secretary General,' while the official ILO officeholder list gives David A. Morse as Director-General through 1970 and Hearman identifies Ruslan with SOBSI/WFTU offices.
confidence: High that the title is inconsistent with ILO officeholder records; medium-high that it is a report error or conflation
basis_and_limitations: This does not establish all of Ruslan's union titles; the likely conflation may involve SOBSI General Secretary or WFTU activity.
next_verification: Check the original Amnesty report and source notes, WFTU leadership lists and SOBSI congress records; do not repeat the ILO title as fact.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Cornell's WFTU finding aid catalogs a 1953 Congress report on colonial and semi-colonial trade unions with Ruslan Widjajasastra as reporter.
confidence: High that the indexed finding-aid entry names Ruslan and the report; no confidence about report contents
basis_and_limitations: The guide's old URL now redirects; the Box 3, Folder 9 contents and report have not been read.
next_verification: Search Cornell's new archives catalog and request Box 3 Folder 9; obtain the report itself and compare name/title variants.

atomic_claim_or_observation: ANRI's 1955 photo inventory catalogs a 9 January SOBSI congress-opening photograph and names Ruslan Widjajasastra and Ny. Munir among participants.
confidence: High that the inventory entry lists these names; no direct visual-identification confidence
basis_and_limitations: The photograph image was not opened; the inventory is not a biographical or attendance register.
next_verification: Open the image and neighboring congress files; compare with SOBSI proceedings and family/photo records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A 2023 military-law journal article gives case-number leads for Ismail Bakri and Ruslan, but the original judgments were not located in the searches reviewed.
claim_type: Archival/legal retrieval lead and failed search
confidence: High that the article/search index gives these locators; no confidence that they reproduce the full case captions accurately
basis_and_limitations: The article PDF returned 404 and the cited judgments were not accessed; case numbers must remain locator leads, not findings.
next_verification: Search Supreme Court and military court archives, Mahkamah Agung catalogs, legal repositories, ANRI and relevant military law libraries.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Amnesty's April 1995 trade-union report labels Ruslan 'former Secretary General of the ILO,' a claim not corroborated by official ILO officeholder records or the opened SOBSI/WFTU scholarship.
confidence: High that the Amnesty report uses the label and that opened ILO history does not list Ruslan; medium-high that it is a misidentification
basis_and_limitations: The label might reflect inaccurate translation or conflation in the advocacy report; avoid attributing intentional deception.
next_verification: Inspect the full Amnesty report and its cited sources; search Indonesian union rosters and ILO archives for any distinct staff post.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman's 2024 article attributes to former SOBSI leader Adam Soepardjan the claim that more than 500 detainees died of starvation in Surabaya's Kalisosok prison in 1968.
confidence: High that the article reports Soepardjan's claim; medium-to-low for the count absent a prison roster
basis_and_limitations: The article says Soepardjan drew on firsthand experience and research but no person-level list or independent count was inspected. Do not treat it as an audited number.
next_verification: Find prison registers, death records, survivor notebooks, family lists, local hospital/cemetery records and Soepardjan's original prison notebooks.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 1961 NSC/Pauker and 2024 WFTU articles add contextual leads but do not provide a nationwide, ethnicity-coded victim roster; the searches reviewed still cannot support a national victim percentage for Javanese, Balinese, Sundanese, Madurese, Chinese or other groups.
confidence: High that no such roster appears in the reviewed materials; not a claim that no dataset exists anywhere
basis_and_limitations: Reviewed materials include regional estimates and partial lists with different units; 1961 census data lack an ethnicity question, and regional population-loss rates are not victim ethnicity shares.
next_verification: Continue seeking provincial/civil victim registers, self-identified ethnicity fields, census microdata, burial and family lists; require common period, category, denominator and de-duplication.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Suryadinata, Arifin and Ananta state that Indonesian population censuses from 1961 through 1990 contained no direct ethnicity question and that the 2000 census was the first to include direct ethnic-composition data.
claim_type: Demographic-method fact, reported by scholarly demographic study
confidence: High that the authors make this conclusion; high for the reviewed census series
basis_and_limitations: The study reviews published census materials and says earlier ethnicity estimates depended on the 1930 census or indirect proxies such as language and religion.
next_verification: Compare the full 1961 census questionnaire and tables with BPS field manuals; retain any provincial or special survey exceptions separately.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The official BPS catalogue confirms a 1961 Indonesian population census publication released on 6 June 1962, but the catalogue abstract does not list an ethnicity variable.
confidence: High for title, date and catalogue description; low for any inference from the abstract about every variable in the book
basis_and_limitations: A catalogue record is metadata, not the full census questionnaire or tabulation volume.
next_verification: Download and inspect the complete census publication and any original questionnaire.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The reviewed materials still do not provide a deduplicated national victim roster with person-level ethnicity, common event-period coding and a matched population denominator; national ethnic shares among those killed therefore remain uncalculable from this archive.
confidence: High about the materials reviewed; not a claim that no such source exists anywhere
basis_and_limitations: Regional event lists, rough totals, detention lists, population-loss estimates and post-1967 expulsions use different units and cannot be combined into national victim shares.
next_verification: Search local victim/family lists and provincial records; require identity, event, period, ethnicity source, denominator, deduplication and inclusion rules.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Cribb and Coppel estimate roughly 2,000 ethnic Chinese deaths against an overall estimate near 500,000 and an approximate 2% Chinese population share, and argue that this does not show national overrepresentation; Woolgar reports a similar national-level conclusion while documenting harassment and regional violence.
claim_type: Contested national estimate and scholarly interpretation
confidence: High that these scholars state the estimates and interpretation; medium-to-low for the underlying counts and comparison
basis_and_limitations: Woolgar, printed p.1977, reports the approximate 2,000 estimate and its national comparison at footnotes 110–112; neither figure is drawn from a complete ethnicity-coded victim register. The ratio is an estimate-based comparison, not an observed victim proportion.
next_verification: Inspect article footnotes and underlying provincial estimates; compare with any national-level records and alternative scholarship.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Melvin argues that documentary and testimonial records in Aceh show episodes of violence in which ethnic-Chinese identity was a targeting factor, challenging a blanket claim that ethnicity never shaped the killings; this regional evidence does not establish a nationwide ethnic percentage.
confidence: High that the article makes the argument; medium for each event pending original archival documents and witness recordings
basis_and_limitations: Melvin’s evidence is geographically bounded and does not yield a nationwide denominator; Cribb and Coppel’s national-level argument and Melvin’s local evidence answer different questions.
next_verification: Inspect the cited KOHANDA files and testimony records; identify victims and distinguish targeted killing, expulsion, detention and property violence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports that South Blitar cells were organized in small three-person groups with differentiated tasks including organization, education/outreach and armed struggle; interviewees’ evidence indicates regrouping and contact work remained central.
claim_type: Scholarly reconstruction from oral histories and trial / military materials
confidence: High that the article reports this structure; medium for exact prevalence and operation across all cells
basis_and_limitations: Hearman, printed pp.79–80 and notes 100–101, cites interviews with Winata and Tuti; she explicitly says exact cell activities are difficult to establish and limits the inference mainly to identifying/reconnecting with cadres and supporters. One interview does not define every unit.
next_verification: Locate surviving cell members’ testimony, committee records, communications and individual trial files.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports Rewang’s account that arms could come from military deserters, theft and black-market purchase, while the military said it found 34 firearms, some old, and a few blowpipes in two captured youth detachments.
claim_type: Retrospective oral testimony juxtaposed with military-reported seizure count
confidence: High that the article records both accounts; medium-to-low for the full weapons inventory
basis_and_limitations: Hearman, printed p.80 and notes 102–106; the seizure count comes from the 1969 military history and no complete arms ledger or independently audited inventory is available. Rewang's proposed supply channels are retrospective testimony.
next_verification: Find Trisula seizure inventories, captured-detachment reports, court exhibits and Rewang’s original interview recording.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports Rewang saying any decision to undertake armed conflict should be democratically approved at a meeting of provincial committees; no minutes or signed resolution for such a meeting were inspected.
claim_type: Retrospective testimony about a proposed decision procedure
confidence: High that the interview reports this statement; low-to-medium that the described procedure was implemented
basis_and_limitations: Hearman, printed p.80 and note 104, records Rewang's interview statement. It is neither a contemporaneous rule nor proof a provincial-committee meeting occurred; other survivor accounts differ. No minutes, signed resolution or independent participant confirmation was located.
next_verification: Search surviving provincial committee records, correspondence, cell reports and testimony from other participants.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The South Blitar article juxtaposes military claims of armed training, Rewang’s account of negligible arms and slow preparation, and former fugitives’ denials of plans to attack; the evidence does not support collapsing the base into either a mature army or a wholly non-political refuge.
confidence: High that these competing accounts are present; medium for the extent and timing of preparation
basis_and_limitations: Military reporting, defendant’s plea and survivor interviews have different incentives and vantage points; no comprehensive party or military operational file was located.
next_verification: Triangulate with full trial exhibits, captured documents, oral histories and local civilian records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Ong’s working paper dates CPM preparations to revive armed struggle to 1967 and its formal announcement to 1 June 1968; its account attributes the 1961 reorientation partly to Chin Peng’s later recollection of Deng Xiaoping’s persuasion.
confidence: High for the paper’s stated dates; medium for the exact internal decision path
basis_and_limitations: The 1961 influence claim is attributed through Chin Peng’s memoir, and the paper also uses Malaysian security officials; it is not a CPM minute.
next_verification: Locate CPM congress/plenum documents, Chin Peng and Rashid Maidin memoirs, Thai border command records and Malaysian intelligence files.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A village case study in Northeast Thailand identifies 7 August 1965 as the first deadly clash later commemorated locally as “First Gunfire Day”; this is a local commemorative chronology, not proof that all CPT armed activity began nationally that day.
confidence: High that the village study reports the local date and commemoration; medium for its designation as a national insurgency onset
basis_and_limitations: The study is a single-village case with interviews, not a complete CPT operational chronology.
next_verification: Compare provincial security records, CPT histories and other regions’ first-clash chronologies.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Bob Bergin’s retrospective study says the CPT had announced armed-struggle doctrine earlier but began its sustained insurgency in 1965; it describes rural recruitment, limited Chinese assistance as recounted by a Thai intelligence official, and a Thai People’s Liberation Army established in late 1968.
claim_type: Retrospective counterinsurgency history with attributed estimates and testimony
confidence: High that the article states these points; medium for exact force size and assistance quantities
basis_and_limitations: The study relies on Thai security perspectives and the author explicitly disclaims official US endorsement; its account is not a neutral party archive.
next_verification: Compare CPT internal histories, Voice of the People of Thailand broadcasts, Thai regional military records and Chinese archives.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The CPB was already a long-running insurgent party before 1965; on 1 January 1968 its forces crossed from China into northeast Burma and opened a border-based campaign that differed structurally from the PKI’s previous public mass-party organization.
confidence: High for the dated UCDP event narrative and CPB’s pre-1965 insurgency; medium for the comparative characterization
basis_and_limitations: The comparison distinguishes organizational form; UCDP is a dataset narrative and Peng’s article principally covers 1969 onward.
next_verification: Review CPB congress and operational documents, Burmese archives, Chinese border records and organizational rosters.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Zhang’s study follows two Beijing youths who joined the CPB army and finds their motives included political danger, escape from difficult rural resettlement and hopes for personal/family security, complicating a purely ideological account of Chinese volunteers.
claim_type: Peer-reviewed biographical interpretation from two cases
confidence: High for these two life histories; low for generalizing the motives to all volunteers
basis_and_limitations: Two biographies and interviews cannot establish the composition or total size of the volunteer force.
next_verification: Compare other volunteers’ oral histories, Chinese sent-down youth records, CPB personnel files and family correspondence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The UCDP Burma–Shan profile describes CPB military expansion through alliances and recruitment among several borderland ethnic groups, while also recording disputes with some ethnic armed actors; this was not a homogeneous national party-army model.
confidence: High that the dataset and scholarly article identify an ethnically diverse border arena; medium on each alliance and strength without cited local records
basis_and_limitations: “Ethnic group” and political affiliation are not interchangeable; boundaries and alliances shifted by time and locality.
next_verification: Trace each alliance to dated CPB, Kachin, Kokang, Wa and Shan records and separate membership from tactical cooperation.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 1968 re-established CPP’s own program called for a peasant-led armed force and rural base areas; its congress documents prove the party’s declared strategy, not the size or maturity of the force in 1968.
claim_type: Party program statement with implementation limit
confidence: High for the text of the program; medium for its contemporaneous implementation
basis_and_limitations: The party texts are political programs and later digital reproductions; organizational capacity requires independent records.
next_verification: Compare the CPP founding congress materials, first NPA roster, Huk veterans’ records, military reports and local land/organizing histories.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The Communist Party of the Philippines was re-established in December 1968 and the New People’s Army was founded in 1969, according to the scholarly account and the party’s contemporary program sequence.
confidence: High for the standard dates; medium for exact initial personnel and operational strength
basis_and_limitations: Program ratification and later scholarship establish dates, but initial troop counts vary by source and should not be compared directly with mass-party membership figures.
next_verification: Check the founding congress communiqué, 1969 NPA declaration, military records and member biographies.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The contemporaneous 1968 US NIE treated Thailand, Burma, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines as different insurgency conditions, but its strength estimates are not standardized and reflect a US intelligence-policy frame.
confidence: High that the NIE makes these assessments; low-to-medium for estimated force numbers and causal judgments
basis_and_limitations: The report’s language is Cold War strategic analysis and several estimates have no common definition of combatant, sympathizer, armed cadre or territorial influence.
next_verification: Compare its cited embassy and intelligence reporting with each party’s records and country-specific scholarship.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Peng’s archival study cautions against treating CPB support as a single fixed Chinese-state policy: it finds Yunnan border counties continued practical aid and border access even as central policy shifted from the mid-1970s.
claim_type: Peer-reviewed archival interpretation of foreign-support mechanism
confidence: High that the study advances this finding; medium pending independent inspection of cited Yunnan files
basis_and_limitations: This concerns the CPB and Yunnan after 1968, not Chinese assistance to the PKI or any operation in Indonesia.
next_verification: Inspect cited Yunnan Border Foreign Affairs Office files and compare them with Beijing central directives, CPB requests and Burmese diplomatic records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: KontraS and ICTJ describe a documentation project begun in February 2011 that created event-based records and conducted interviews with victims/witnesses in Blitar and Buton.
period: 2011–2012; Indonesia, with field work in Blitar and Buton
confidence: High that the report describes this method; medium that the resulting database exhaustively represents the two regions
basis_and_limitations: The report states its own project design and advocacy purpose; the underlying full database and interview set were not opened.
next_verification: Request the project protocol, database schema, full interview index and any anonymization/verification rules.

atomic_claim_or_observation: KontraS’s report says Munir and Ruslan joined the East Java regional committee in late 1966 and, with secretary Suwandi, went to South Blitar in March 1967 to begin implementing the project committee.
period: Late 1966–March 1967; East Java and South Blitar
claim_type: Later documentary reconstruction based on anonymous interviews and participant materials
confidence: High that the report gives this sequence; medium for the precise dates and full group movement
basis_and_limitations: The report cites anonymous interview codes FC/HCC and Munir’s 1973 defense; those interviews and the original court text were not inspected here. This may describe different arrivals/implementation stages than other accounts.
next_verification: Obtain the report’s interview key/recordings where available, Munir plea original, and Rewang/other participants’ dated travel accounts.

atomic_claim_or_observation: In André Liem’s account, Rewang recalled proposing a move out of Jakarta after Sudisman’s arrest; the proposal was accepted, and East Java contacts had prepared a village considered suitable for a base.
period: After December 1966; Jakarta to South Blitar
claim_type: Retrospective participant testimony recorded in oral-history research
confidence: High that Liem records this recollection; medium for the exact collective decision and timing
basis_and_limitations: Liem’s chapter relies largely on 2000 interviews and some military documents; no CC minutes or dated transfer order was located.
next_verification: Inspect Rewang’s complete memoir/interview recording, East Java regional correspondence and any evacuation or project-committee instructions.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Rewang told Liem that the underground leadership had formed an emergency CC, provincial leaderships, project committees and the beginnings of guerrilla detachments, while discussing when armed struggle could formally begin.
period: 1967–1968; South Blitar and other proposed Java bases
claim_type: Retrospective participant testimony about organization and procedure
confidence: High that the interview text says this; medium for the exact completeness and operational reach of the structures
basis_and_limitations: Liem reports that rosters were deliberately compartmentalized and interviewees could not identify all personnel; no complete party list or minutes were found.
next_verification: Find CC/Kompro rosters, appointment notes, meeting records, courier reports and dated unit returns.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Rewang said a fully organized armed struggle would begin only after the project committees were ready and a national conference had reviewed party reorganization and political conditions; he described the timing as still under discussion.
claim_type: Retrospective testimony about declared decision procedure
confidence: High that Rewang made this account; medium for whether every local unit knew or followed that rule
basis_and_limitations: The national conference and its proposed review have not been located in a contemporaneous record; his recollection may summarize formal policy after the defeat.
next_verification: Locate draft conference convocations, CC circulars, provincial committee minutes and reports from local detachments.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Rewang characterized some local disarmings and attacks against people he called “executioners” as actions outside the CC program and as premature actions that could alert the Army.
period: Late 1967–early 1968; South Blitar and nearby districts
claim_type: Retrospective participant account and strategic interpretation
confidence: High that Liem records this statement; medium that the actions lacked all higher-level knowledge or approval
basis_and_limitations: This is Rewang’s later explanation, not an extant order or a complete account of every operation; actors and motives varied by incident.
next_verification: Build an incident-by-incident table from local testimony, captured case files, Army intelligence chronology, court exhibits and any underground orders.

atomic_claim_or_observation: KontraS’s report describes a reorganized leadership in which Ruslan headed the Politbiro, Rewang led Agitprop and Munir led armed struggle; it says Munir completed the Perjuta concept in early September 1967 for circulation to other bases.

next_verification: Locate the original Perjuta text, dispatch/courier records, CC appointments and source interviews behind FC/HCC.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A Koran Sulindo article quoting Rewang’s 2017 memoir dates the emergency CC meeting to 23 May 1967 and names Ruslan as chair, with organizational work, Agitprop and armed-struggle departments assigned respectively to Ruslan, Rewang and Munir.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Arah Juang lists Tjugito, Iskandar Subekti, Sukatno and Suwandi among the emergency CC members and separately names Ruslan, Oloan Hutapea, Rewang and Munir as a new Politbiro.

next_verification: Compare with full memoir, KontraS source interviews, organization papers in trials, military capture rosters and dated internal party documents.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Koran Sulindo reports that a South Blitar guerrilla detachment had 150 armed fighters intended eventually to form a regular force.

atomic_claim_or_observation: KontraS’s report says Tjugito and Pratomo prepared a guerrilla-training text titled “Memimpin Perang Rakyat”; Tirto repeats this association.
claim_type: Later report and journalism, with source dependence unresolved

atomic_claim_or_observation: Koran Sulindo says the Army obtained more specific South Blitar intelligence after the December 1967 arrest of a person it names Kusno/Yudo and after Pratomo’s capture, then used the information to target the underground network.

next_verification: Obtain the relevant Trisula intelligence reports, arrest/interrogation records, Pratomo case file, and match names/dates against the official operation history.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Koran Sulindo, summarizing M. Jasin’s memoir, says the Trisula operation initially lacked central funding, that Jasin borrowed 20 million rupiah from East Java governor Mohammad Noer, that an Air Force commander contributed two companies, and that Jakarta funding arrived later.

next_verification: Inspect Jasin’s memoir pages, Kodam budget and requisition records, provincial treasury entries, Air Force orders and central transfer documentation.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Liem’s chapter distinguishes South Blitar refugees gathering in 1966–67 and preparations beginning in early 1967 from the official New Order version it quotes, which says the PKI only began forming the South Blitar Kompro in October 1967.

confidence: High that Liem records this contrast; medium on the underlying formal start dates
basis_and_limitations: Liem, printed p.164, says the chapter’s interview and reconstruction differ from the official military chronology; he does not reproduce a dated party decree or the complete underlying military document. “Refugees arrived,” “site preparation,” and “formal Kompro formation” may be separate events.
next_verification: Read the cited 1969 Semdam and 1968 Skets Masa histories page by page; find dated Kompro/CC records, captured files, Rewang memoir pages and travel/communications records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Rewang recalled that after Sudisman was arrested in December 1966 he proposed leaving Jakarta for village areas to reorganize and prepare resistance; he said the proposal was accepted and East Java contacts had prepared a village considered suitable as a base.
claim_type: Retrospective participant testimony reproduced in oral-history chapter
confidence: High that Rewang gave this account as reproduced by Liem; medium for the exact sequence and timing

next_verification: Obtain the Rewang recording/transcript, the named East Java contact’s testimony, and dated travel or committee records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Liem reports Rewang’s recollection that roughly nine PKI Central Committee members, East Java regional figures and cadres from other areas began work in the project committees, while their structure and membership were compartmentalized.
period: 1967; South Blitar and other proposed bases
confidence: High that the chapter gives this approximate composition; medium for the number and full membership
basis_and_limitations: Liem, printed pp.177–178, attributes the account to Rewang and Muyatno. No dated attendance list or complete roster is available; the chapter itself notes that participants often did not know other members.
next_verification: Compare names with the full memoir, captured lists, trial records and independent testimony; do not assume “nine” counts every CC member or all arrivals.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Liem says the intended Kompro structure extended from district to village, while the “neat” chart shown in military publications may overstate how complete or consistently functioning the underground organization was.
claim_type: Comparison of confiscated military material with survivor interviews and historian assessment
confidence: High that Liem makes this methodological comparison; medium for how far the military chart overstates actual functioning
basis_and_limitations: Liem, printed pp.177–178, says the military’s organizational chart presents a clear, effective structure but interviewees’ recollections suggest more limited and compartmentalized organization. The underlying confiscated papers and the cited military volume were not directly re-examined in this pass.
next_verification: Inspect the 1969 military history and captured documents; determine when each chart was created, which units existed on paper, and which were active.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports that some South Blitar participants described three-person cells responsible for organization, education/outreach and armed-struggle work, each linked to an outside contact; she says the cells’ exact activities are difficult to establish beyond locating and reconnecting with members and supporters.
claim_type: Retrospective oral-history reconstruction with explicit limits
confidence: High that the cited interviews and article describe this structure; medium for prevalence and uniformity across the base
basis_and_limitations: Hearman cites interviews with Winata and Tuti and an anonymous contact, and explicitly cautions that the cells’ activities cannot be reconstructed precisely. This is not a full organizational manual or proof every cadre belonged to a cell.
next_verification: Obtain interview transcripts/recordings, identify cells only where sources permit, and compare with captured papers and trial exhibits.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports that a local participant described cell work as identifying and regrouping with party members and sympathizers in surrounding areas; this supports a network-rebuilding function but does not establish that every cell conducted armed operations.
claim_type: Historian’s bounded inference from participant interviews
confidence: High that Hearman states this; medium for how representative the described cell was
basis_and_limitations: The article says it is difficult to determine what cells did beyond identifying and reconnecting cadres and supporters. The evidence is a limited set of interviews and does not describe every cell or command relationship.
next_verification: Seek cell-specific reports, correspondence, training records and interviews from people in different roles and project sites.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Muyatno told Liem that South Blitar military training described to him remained limited to political/ideological study and practical skills such as knife-throwing, ambush and self-defence; a planned Malang Selatan school and war-cadre courses are described as plans, not demonstrated completed institutions.
claim_type: Retrospective participant testimony and reported organizational plans
confidence: High that Liem records this testimony and plans; medium for the total training delivered across all units
basis_and_limitations: Liem, printed pp.178–179, attributes basic skills and the distinction between plans and operating schools to Muyatno. Nearby interviews describe Maoist “village encircles city”/people’s war theory, a 10:1 guerrilla-force rule and Vietnamese tunnel experience as subjects discussed, not measured capabilities. No instructor rosters, attendance lists, course materials or school operation records were opened.
next_verification: Search captured materials, military interrogation files, student lists, training notes and the original manuals; distinguish plan from completed course.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Rewang told Liem that caves and dug shelters in South Blitar were small, sporadic and unfinished, intended chiefly for refuge rather than combat; he described a long-term plan to connect shelters while building the party, using Vietnam as a model.
claim_type: Retrospective participant testimony about shelters and strategy
confidence: High that Rewang made this statement as reproduced by Liem; medium for the extent and use of all shelters
basis_and_limitations: Liem, printed pp.179–180, records Rewang’s recollection that the shelters were still initial, not connected and used to hide/protect people. Military depictions of a coherent underground network vary; no mapped shelter survey or full infrastructure inventory was examined.
next_verification: Compare military maps and photographs, local cave/shelter surveys, captured engineering notes and testimony from residents and different cadres.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Liem records Rewang’s claim that children and older residents sometimes carried warnings or messages and that some local protection was voluntary; the same chapter records farmer Ruslan saying a village head ordered him and other men to carry military packs and supplies, while Hearman describes couriers, escorts, evacuation and other compelled civilian logistics.
claim_type: Competing participant testimony and oral-history reconstruction about local support
confidence: High that these accounts are reported; medium for the frequency and voluntariness of support across communities
basis_and_limitations: Accounts refer to different people and actions. Rewang’s general description cannot stand for every resident; Ruslan’s single account concerns a specific military party and route-mapping excursion. Hearman records additional assistance and pressure, but the underlying military and village rosters are absent. Do not turn either account into unanimous support or opposition.
next_verification: Build village-specific evidence from resident interviews, evacuation and administrative rosters, courier/contact testimony, and military reports.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports divergent testimony about whether fugitives in South Blitar intended or participated in violence: some interviewees denied involvement or described refuge/family reunion, while others acknowledged that selected attacks, weapons theft or armed actions occurred.
claim_type: Historian’s comparison of conflicting survivor testimony
confidence: High that Hearman documents divergent testimony; low-to-medium for the prevalence and precise scope of actions
basis_and_limitations: Interviewees had different roles, information and legal/personal risks; Hearman notes that some actions were not widely acknowledged. Testimony does not establish command authorization, a universal movement policy or exact casualty totals.
next_verification: Match each alleged action to dated district/police/military files, victim and family testimony, court exhibits and party communications.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports that military evacuations in June 1968 moved thousands of residents from hamlets and villages into temporary holding camps for several days; one cited military-history example covers 22 June–5 July and names 12 village meeting points.
claim_type: Oral-history reconstruction cross-referenced to an official military history
confidence: High that the article reports this and identifies its page-based source; medium for the full population count and each site’s actual occupancy
basis_and_limitations: Hearman, printed p.85 and note 139 cites Semdam VIII/Brawidjaja, Operasi Trisula, p.206, for a 22 June–5 July example with twelve named village meeting points; the article also cites Mrs. J.'s interview for warnings in camps. The military book, evacuee registers and camp occupancy lists were not directly reviewed.
next_verification: Read p.206 and adjacent pages; locate village orders, household lists, camp registers, return dates and testimony from each named site.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman says speeches in the holding camps warned residents not to assist communists or they would be killed, and aircraft dropped leaflets with similar messages.
confidence: High that Hearman reports this account; medium until the underlying leaflet, order or independent testimony is inspected
basis_and_limitations: The speech claim is footnoted to an interview with Mrs. J.; the underlying leaflets and operation instructions were not retrieved.
next_verification: Locate leaflet originals/photos, air-tasking orders, camp briefing scripts, and accounts from additional named villages.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Liem records two separately interviewed local witnesses, Paijo and Maryono, describing soldiers bringing roughly forty male detainees to a South Blitar riverside, shooting them and compelling local men to bury or handle the bodies; Paijo describes bound detainees and a threat against the eleven forced laborers, while Maryono recalls eight victims put in a cave and thirty-two buried in two pits.
claim_type: Specific witness testimony recorded by a later oral-history study
confidence: High that both interviews are separately recorded and concern the same reported episode; medium for the event particulars absent contemporary records, named victim verification or forensic evidence.
basis_and_limitations: Hearman, printed pp.83–84 and notes 133–138 reproduces Paijo's account; Liem's chapter separately records Paijo and Maryono interviews. These remain retrospective oral accounts with approximate counts and no victim-by-victim roster, forensic survey or contemporaneous operational log.
next_verification: Locate the original ISSI recordings/transcripts; identify the site without merging locality variants; seek family testimony, burial/missing-person records, forensic survey and military/camp registers; verify each remembered name and whether the cave/pits belong to this same event.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports that Suwandi, East Java regional secretary, was arrested on 12 June 1968 and paraded at public meetings urging people to surrender; the paper also reports a museum photograph showing him bound during interrogation.
claim_type: Scholar’s reconstruction from a military history, participant accounts and a museum photograph
confidence: High that Hearman documents the arrest date and public appeals; medium for the sequence pending direct file review
basis_and_limitations: Hearman cites the military history and interviews; a witness reported hearing that Suwandi had been tortured for three days, which is an allegation, not a verified interrogation record. The photograph caption labels him as under interrogation but does not by itself establish when or how he was treated.
next_verification: Inspect the cited operation-history pages, Suwandi’s arrest/interrogation and court file, original photograph/caption provenance, and independent testimony.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman says the Brawijaya military history characterized the July–early August 1968 arrest wave as the product of “tactical interrogations,” a method said to induce detainees to cooperate with authorities.

confidence: High that Hearman cites this term to the army history; low-to-medium for what the procedure entailed in each interrogation
basis_and_limitations: Hearman cites pp.137 and 140 of the military history; the underlying text, interview logs, coercion protocols and interrogation records were not opened. The label may be euphemistic or operationally specific; do not infer voluntariness from the term.
next_verification: Read the cited pages and original interrogation reports; compare detainee testimony, physical evidence, legal records and the Army’s own definition of the method.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman, citing the Brawijaya military history, reports that Ruslan Wijajasastra and Munir were captured on 13 July 1968 and Rewang on 20 July; separate Amnesty/TAPOL sources use 14 July for Munir and Ruslan, and a 2017 Tirto profile says Rewang was captured on 21 July.
claim_type: Conflicting capture-date record across military-history citation, later scholarship and human-rights reporting
confidence: High that the sources report these different dates; medium/low for the exact date of capture pending registers
basis_and_limitations: Hearman cites *Operasi Trisula*, pp.137 and 142; Amnesty/TAPOL may record official detention/admission or prison intake rather than field capture. Tirto gives no record image for 21 July. Keep capture, formal arrest, notification and prison registration timestamps separate.
next_verification: Obtain operation logs, capture reports, interrogation booking sheets, prison intake registers, family notifications, trial files and original Amnesty source correspondence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman says that by late August 1968 several senior South Blitar leaders, including Rewang, Ruslan, Iskandar Subekti, Sukatno, Djadiwirosoebroto and Mardjoko, had been transferred to Jakarta for trial.
claim_type: Retrospective participant testimony and historian reconstruction
confidence: High that Hearman reports this transfer; medium for each individual date and destination without transfer registers
basis_and_limitations: The article attributes the timing to Rewang’s interview. Individual trial venues and detention facilities still need to be checked against court dockets and prison registers.
next_verification: Find transfer warrants, Lowokwaru/Madura prison ledgers, Jakarta detention registers, trial summonses and contemporaneous family notices.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Arief, Soedarsono and Sumarno’s 1999 official history says that, after the 1967 leadership change in East Java, some strategically placed or vacant civilian offices—including village head, regent and rector—were temporarily filled by ABRI personnel.
claim_type: Retrospective institutional account of military participation in civilian administration
confidence: High that the report states this; moderate for the scope and duration of appointments because no roster or appointment orders were checked.
basis_and_limitations: Printed p.40. The report names categories but does not list every officeholder or establish that every vacancy was filled by a soldier.
next_verification: Find governor and district appointment decisions, village caretaker lists, dates, and civilian/military chains of command.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 1999 provincial history says Kodam VIII/Brawijaya, acting as the core of the regional Kopkamtib special executive, directed Korems to conduct intelligence and territorial operations with civilian agencies; it describes intelligence as assessing unrest and remaining PKI capacity, and territorial operations as restoring government authority.
claim_type: Retrospective official account of security and civil-military administration
confidence: High for the stated institutional policy and stated aims; moderate for execution and local variation because orders and reports were not inspected.
basis_and_limitations: Printed pp.43–44. The account’s use of “restoring authority” reflects the government’s own administrative framing.
next_verification: Obtain the original Kodam/Korem instructions, Laksus Kopkamtib records, six-hour reporting files, local civil-administration orders, and village-level implementation records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 1999 history describes a separate secret Operation Sambar Raga in Surabaya from January through August 1968 and says authorities arrested 712 people called PKI remnants; its footnote points to Sketsmasa’s 1969 third-edition Trisula booklet, pp.40–41.
claim_type: Retrospective official account; cited military pamphlet not opened
confidence: High that the history reports 712 and cites this pamphlet; low-to-moderate for number, category, and actual operation scope absent registers.
basis_and_limitations: Printed p.44 and note 17. This is Surabaya/Sambar Raga, not a Trisula detainee count and must not be added to the Blitar figure.
next_verification: Locate Sambar Raga orders, arrest and intake registers, Korem Surabaya reporting, Sketsmasa third edition pp.40–41, and individual case records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 1999 official history claims that by late 1967 East Java’s “new-style PKI” had seven urban Triko and eight Kompro networks; it describes Blitar Kompro as having two guerrilla detachments, 17 village guerrilla groups, STPR/KKPR training and distribution of trained cadres elsewhere.
period: Late 1967; East Java and South Blitar
confidence: High that this is the state-sponsored history’s description; low-to-moderate that all listed bodies were active at the stated strength, since rosters, course records and captured documents were not read.
basis_and_limitations: Printed pp.41–42. The report cites official military history for some details and uses the New Order category “PKI gaya baru”; participant-based studies describe uneven preparation, compartmentalization and contested recollection.
next_verification: Compare each named Triko/Kompro, Detga, Gerda and school against party papers, course registers, names, weapons receipts, village testimony and the original military chart; distinguish planned, named, staffed and operational units.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A 1999 East Java history attributes to Kodam commander Major General M. Yasin’s 9 August 1968 Malang press conference an Operation Trisula total of 850 detainees and seizures of 37 firearms and four grenades.
claim_type: Later government history reporting a contemporaneous military announcement
confidence: High that the 1999 history attributes these figures to Yasin; low-to-moderate that the figures are complete or comparable to other totals until the press text and underlying ledgers are found.
basis_and_limitations: Printed p.45. Liem reports a different official figure of 257 arrests for the May–July effective attack period, citing the 1969 Brawijaya book p.127 (C2337). Amnesty International’s 1984 report says Jasin claimed more than 800 arrests in June–July, mainly in South Blitar, and “many” PKI members killed, but gives no death total; this may relay the same official announcement and is not independent verification. The 9 Aug figure is a checkpoint during an operation whose follow-on phases continued; press text and registers remain absent.
next_verification: Find the 9 Aug 1968 press transcript and contemporary Malang/Surabaya newspapers; inspect S1390 p.127 and Trisula arrest lists; define whether counts include surrendered persons, noncombatants, repeat arrests, other operational sectors or the post-July phase.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 1999 provincial history says Trisula proceeded through reconnaissance, destruction, consolidation and clearance; it then places civil-territorial consolidation/rehabilitation through 7 September 1968 and a final territorial-development phase through 16 December.
confidence: High for the chronology printed in this retrospective account; moderate for dates and boundaries until operation orders and closure reports are inspected.
basis_and_limitations: Printed pp.44–45. Its described post-combat phases matter for the period of village administration and surveillance; they should not be collapsed into the named combat phase.
next_verification: Compare PRINOP orders, Trisula command logs, 7 Sep closeout, territorial rehabilitation instructions, and 16 Dec final-phase records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: S1392’s 1999 chapter describes the 1967–68 consolidation as a project to restore governmental authority and later “New Orderization”; its introduction frames the New Order development era as overcoming crises attributed to the Old Order and the G30S/PKI rebellion.
claim_type: Official memory and political framing in a government-sponsored history
confidence: High for the text’s framing; this is evidence of later state historiography, not independent proof of the allegations or the success claimed.
basis_and_limitations: Introduction printed p.1 and chapter 3 printed pp.39–45; its citation base includes official military and national histories.
next_verification: Compare with 1960s orders and press, provincial civilian records, village-level accounts, and later state commemorative materials; trace how wording and classifications change by edition.

atomic_claim_or_observation: S1392’s bibliography lists a third edition of Sketsmasa’s Operasi Trisula, published by Grip in Surabaya in 1969, citing pp.34 and 40–41; this differs from the 1968 second edition listed in the NII/CiNii catalogue (S1391).
confidence: High for the two different bibliographic statements; low for edition contents and pagination until copies are collated.
basis_and_limitations: S1391 is a catalogue record for a 44-page second edition; S1392 printed p.55 cites a third edition. Same title and publisher do not establish that text or pagination is identical.
next_verification: Request both editions from IDE-JETRO/NII or Japanese/Indonesian library networks; compare title pages, contents, print statements, pagination and cited claims.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman’s 2010 scholarly article says the 1969 Brawijaya Trisula volume was fast-tracked for publication on 1 October 1969, the fourth anniversary of the coup attempt.
claim_type: Secondary source statement about an official military publication
confidence: High that Hearman makes this statement; moderate for the exact imprint date until the book’s title page/colophon is inspected.
basis_and_limitations: The book itself has not been opened. “Fast-tracked for publication” is the historian’s statement, not a verified title-page or print-shop date.
next_verification: Acquire the volume and inspect title page, colophon, edition and production files; compare the claimed date with any accession/receipt records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman’s 2010 and 2017 accounts cite the 11 August 1968 NYT report for Trisula-era figures, but render the figure differently: about 2,000 “party members” captured/killed or killed, alongside arrests/detention and displacement. Her 2018 essay returns to the captured-or-killed wording and notes that local villagers were likely included; the original newspaper remains inaccessible.
period: 1968 figures as presented in 2010 and 2017 scholarship
claim_type: Cross-version comparison of a cited contemporary press count
confidence: High that Hearman’s publications present these formulations and cite the same NYT item; low for the precise number and fate categories because the newspaper and any roster are unavailable.
basis_and_limitations: Do not treat three Hearman texts as independent corroboration: they derive from one author’s research and the same NYT/Army reporting chain. The 2017 “2,000 killed” wording conflicts with the 2010/2018 captured-or-killed formulation; categories cannot be reconciled without the underlying article and method.
next_verification: Retrieve the 11 August 1968 NYT text and any Army briefing/operation registers; keep killed, captured, arrested, detained and displaced separate and check civilian inclusion.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Amnesty International’s 1984 report says East Java commander Jasin claimed that more than 800 Communists had been arrested during June and July 1968, mainly in South Blitar, and that many PKI members had been killed.
claim_type: Human-rights report relaying a military commander’s claim
confidence: High that Amnesty reports this claim; low as independent verification of either the arrest count or killings.
basis_and_limitations: The report gives no number of deaths and does not identify an underlying press article in this paragraph. It may descend from the same Jasin announcement later reported as 850 detainees; this is not an independent count.
next_verification: Locate Jasin’s statement and contemporary Malang/Surabaya reports; reconcile “more than 800 arrested,” “850 detainees,” count cut-off, geography and whether deaths are separate.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman 2010 says around 1,000 “party members” were captured or killed in a passage on Trisula, but footnote 61 gives Philip Shabecoff’s NYT article date as 13 February 1968, before the operation. Les Evans’s 3 March 1969 article says the 29 October 1968 NYT report put killed-or-captured at 2,000 and a mid-February follow-up cut that number in half, making the printed year a likely citation anomaly.
period: 1968-02-13 citation in a later account of May–September 1968 events
confidence: High that Hearman prints the 1,000 figure and footnote date, and that Evans reports a mid-February follow-up after October 1968; low for the original NYT date, exact wording and what the 1,000 measured.
basis_and_limitations: Evans is a derivative, politically committed newspaper account, not the original NYT article. The article page remains blocked. “Likely citation anomaly” is a chronological inference, not a bibliographic correction. Do not use 1,000 as a Trisula death total.
next_verification: Read the NYT TimesMachine/ProQuest/microfilm article, verify the issue date and paragraph context, and inspect Hearman’s original notes or an erratum.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman 2017 reports that Jasin described PKI political support in South Blitar as very high before October 1965, citing p.8 of his 1968 parliamentary briefing.
period: Before 1965-10; South Blitar; claim reported in 2017
claim_type: A military commander’s retrospective statement, quoted by a historian
confidence: High that Hearman reports and cites the statement; moderate-to-low as a measure of actual support because the briefing and any underlying survey are unavailable.
basis_and_limitations: The source is a command briefing rather than an election or membership census. It cannot establish a percentage in 1968 or show how every village related to the underground base.
next_verification: Obtain Jasin’s briefing p.8; compare 1955 election results by subdistrict, party/mass-organization records, 1961 census limits and village-level oral histories.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports that U.S. Consul D. T. Kenney and another consular official praised Trisula during a June 1969 visit as a counterinsurgency success while describing South Blitar as a “soft target.”
claim_type: Scholarly report of a diplomatic field assessment
confidence: High that Hearman reports the cable’s assessment; no evidence this demonstrates U.S. participation in planning or conducting Trisula.
basis_and_limitations: The June 29 airgram itself was not accessed; this is a year-after-operation assessment cited by a historian.
next_verification: Retrieve the full airgram and identify the officials, itinerary, interlocutors, operational access, and any follow-up decisions.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A 2016 study citing the 29 June 1969 U.S. consular airgram reports that Kenney recommended food-for-work assistance, believing poverty reduction could deter renewed communist infiltration; the airgram also described government resettlement along roads to facilitate control.
claim_type: U.S. consular policy advice as quoted/paraphrased in scholarship
confidence: High that Hearman reports this recommendation and resettlement statement; low that any U.S. funds were authorized or delivered.
basis_and_limitations: The original cable, U.S. aid decision, Indonesian request, budget, shipment, implementing agency and recipient list were not obtained. Advice is not implementation.
next_verification: Read airgram pp.2 and 5; search AID/State/USOM food-for-work records, Jakarta/Surabaya decisions, Indonesian labor/social-affairs plans, disbursements and local project registers.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A 1971 IKIP Surabaya/Balai Penelitian Pendidikan report on a foster-care survey for children affected by G30S/PKI in South Blitar and prospective foster families in Bagor, Nganjuk and Blitar municipality is cited by Hearman; her article connects the report to efforts to place children orphaned during Trisula with new families. Suwandi’s 1985 thesis says the 1971 pilot concerned children who lost both parents and reports child removals from prior family environments in two grandmother cases.

confidence: High that the report is cited and the article describes such a policy; low for the number of children, how placements were administered, consent and long-term results.
basis_and_limitations: No copy of the 1971 report or child-specific register was accessed. “Orphaned” and “lost both parents” may describe a narrower pilot group, not all children affected by Trisula. The thesis offers ethnographic cases from 1980 fieldwork, while both survey citations remain secondary references; no child-level totals or case records are available.
next_verification: Obtain report and appendices; seek social-affairs case files, consent/guardian forms, birth/family records, placement addresses, return/contact histories and interviews with children and kin.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Raharjo Suwandi says the fieldwork for his ANU thesis ran from October 1979 to March 1981 and identifies 1980 as his Blitar fieldwork year.
claim_type: Methodology/provenance statement in an ethnographic thesis

basis_and_limitations: Printed preliminary pages and p.5. The thesis was completed June 1985.
next_verification: Check field notebooks/interview dates if exact timing of individual South Blitar accounts matters.

atomic_claim_or_observation: In his retrospective South Blitar account, Suwandi describes children of peasants killed in the violence being taken from their prior family environment; he gives two grandmother cases, one whose grandson and another whose two grandchildren were removed, and says one grandmother tried to reclaim them.
period: Reported in 1985 thesis about events in the 1970s; South Blitar
confidence: High that the thesis reports these cases; moderate as evidence of the particular experiences because names, dates and administrative records are absent. It does not establish a count for all children or every placement.
basis_and_limitations: Printed pp.173–174. Suwandi uses “forced adoption” as his description; he records one local authority’s “sinful environment” phrase. The report is ethnographic, based on Blitar fieldwork in 1980, not a contemporaneous case file.
next_verification: Find the 1971 foster-care survey, child/caregiver case files, local social-affairs correspondence, guardianship/placement orders, and interviews with affected children and kin.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Suwandi says a 1971 South Blitar foster-care survey detailed implementation of a pilot affecting children who had lost both parents.
claim_type: Later thesis citation to a government/university survey
confidence: High that the thesis describes the survey this way; low-to-moderate for the pilot’s actual eligibility and scope until the 1971 report is read.
basis_and_limitations: Suwandi printed p.174 identifies the report and the both-parents-lost subset. Hearman 2017 independently supplies a fuller bibliographic title, but both are secondary references to an unaccessed report.
next_verification: Obtain the report and establish numbers, definitions of orphanhood, survey method, funding, consent/guardianship, proposed versus completed placements and outcomes.

atomic_claim_or_observation: NARA describes the Department of State’s 1963–1973 RG 59 central Subject-Numeric File as divided into a 1967–1969 segment that includes airgrams; its box lists identify exact boxes and are available in the Archives II Research Room.
