next_verification: Use RG 59 Subject-Numeric Files, 1967–1969 box lists and request a search under POL 18 INDON / Surabaya / 29 June 1969 / Airgram A-12; record box and document number only after direct inspection.

atomic_claim_or_observation: NARA’s indexed 1965–1973 Department of State classification-manual entry defines POL 18 as “Provincial, Municipal, and State Government.”
claim_type: Official classification-manual entry, available in search-index excerpt
confidence: Moderate: the exact subject label appears in the official NARA-indexed excerpt, but the full manual PDF could not be opened in this session. The classification is a filing category, not an event finding.
basis_and_limitations: The citation “POL 18 INDON” in scholarship may indicate this file category; additional suffixes and exact box/series location remain unresolved.
next_verification: Read the complete manual and inspect the cited document’s header, routing stamps and folder label at NARA before normalizing the archival citation.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman’s 2015 article cites a 1970 Department of Social Affairs/field-survey report titled “Laporan Survey, Masalah Kurang Makan Salah Makan” for Bakung, Sumberdadi and surrounding South Blitar; the article cites its pp.18, 25 and 29.
period: 1970 survey; Bakung, Sumberdadi and surrounding South Blitar
claim_type: Bibliographic record and scholarly citation to an unaccessed primary report
confidence: High that the article cites a report with this title, agency/publisher and page references; moderate for exact institutional wording because the report title page and full text are unavailable.
basis_and_limitations: Hearman’s bibliography gives Yogyakarta and Balai Penelitian dan Peninjauan Sosial; a later bibliography has a variant “Dinas Research Disorganisasi Sosial.” Do not silently standardize the agency name.
next_verification: Search Indonesian government and university catalogs, Ministry of Social Affairs and local archives; request title-page image, full report, questionnaire, tables and appendices.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports that a 1970 government survey gave 1969 sale-crop figures for Bakung and Sumberdadi together: population 2,538; sweet potatoes 25 tonnes, maize 12 tonnes and rice 4 tonnes; she cautions these were marketed quantities and did not appear to include rice/cassava grown for household consumption.
period: 1969 crops; two villages, as reported in 1970 survey
claim_type: Quantitative data reported by a later scholarly article from a government survey
confidence: High that Hearman reports these figures and their market-output interpretation; moderate for the underlying counts until the survey tables and definitions are inspected. The two-village total cannot be generalized to all South Blitar.
basis_and_limitations: Printed article pp.92–93, note 64 cites survey p.25. Distinguish marketed output from total production, household consumption and nutritional adequacy.
next_verification: Obtain survey p.25 and tables; inspect units, harvest period, population denominator, crops for sale versus subsistence, and possible household-level variation.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman quotes the 1970 survey as reporting that surveyed households generally could not afford tea, sugar and coffee and continued to drink unboiled water.
claim_type: Scholarly quotation/transmission of government survey findings
confidence: High that Hearman quotes this statement; moderate for its exact representativeness because the original page, question wording, sample and translation are unavailable. It is not evidence that every household had the same diet or water practice.
basis_and_limitations: Printed p.93, note 69 cites survey p.29. The article reproduces a short English translation from Indonesian.
next_verification: Read report p.29 and questionnaire; identify respondent count, question wording, drinking-water sources and whether the statement is a survey result or narrative generalization.

atomic_claim_or_observation: ANRI’s KOTI inventory item 515 describes a two-leaf copy of RRI broadcast-news notes for 1–3 October 1965, including the Revolution Council list; the catalog also associates it with 28 September 1965.
claim_type: Official archival finding-aid description / retrieval lead
confidence: High for the catalogue description and locator; unresolved for the date discrepancy and unseen contents.
basis_and_limitations: Official inventory PDF, item 515, printed p.69/70. The described broadcast dates postdate the catalog-associated date. It is a copy, two leaves; no folder image or underlying RRI log was examined.
next_verification: Request KOTI item 515; check cover, foliation, copy provenance and attached broadcast notes; compare RRI program logs and contemporary newspaper reproductions.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The Cornell reproduction of Revolution Council Decision No. 1 lists Tjugito as No. 14 under “Communist Group”; the separate scholarly affiliation table and Embassy A-398 roster identify him as a PKI figure and Central Committee member.
period: 1965-10-01; roster reflects the Embassy’s understanding after the May 1965 CC plenary
claim_type: Crosswalk of a reproduced contemporary list and a U.S. diplomatic roster
confidence: High that the reproduced list and A-398 roster contain the name; moderate that the entries refer to the same person and reflect current formal affiliation.
basis_and_limitations: The original movement list reproduced in S253 and Embassy roster in S189 are different documents; the Council-member affiliation table is later scholarly annotation. The PKI Oct. 5 statement said named members were not informed or asked. No evidence establishes Tjugito’s prior knowledge, consent, attendance or operational role.
next_verification: Locate the original Decision No. 1, PKI May-plenum roster/minutes, Tjugito’s own testimony and any Council records; compare name forms and dates.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The CIA’s 1968 report says the PKI Secretariat was told on 26 September that a military action might occur before 5–6 October without a fixed date; Peris Pardede requested and received assignment to Medan, and the report says he was given timing information on 29 September and departed early on 1 October.
claim_type: CIA retrospective account based on interrogation testimony
confidence: High that the CIA report makes this account; moderate-to-low as an independently verified reconstruction.
basis_and_limitations: Printed pp.159–161. The CIA itself says its conspiracy reconstruction depends entirely on interrogations. The report includes Pardede’s reported recollection, but no Secretariat minutes, travel/mission order or independent regional receipt was opened.
next_verification: Obtain the original interrogation/transcript and Pardede trial file; seek PKI Secretariat notes, travel records, Medan CDB minutes and contemporary party communications.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The CIA report says Sudisman briefed CC/PKI member Suwardiningsih about officers’ planned action and the projected Revolutionary Council, then sent her to Palembang; it reports her 1 October arrival, oral instructions to the CDB, mobilization discussions and four meetings on 1, 3, 5 and 6 October.
claim_type: CIA retrospective account attributed to an Army-interrogated PKI member
confidence: High that the CIA report records this narrative; moderate-to-low for the uncorroborated details.
basis_and_limitations: Printed pp.157–160. The report says the account came from Suwardiningsih’s interrogation; it does not provide the original interrogation, party minutes, travel record or Palembang CDB statement. Its narrative must not be treated as independent confirmation of the CIA’s wider interpretation.
next_verification: Locate Suwardiningsih’s trial and interrogation file, travel record, Palembang CDB minutes/support statement, contemporaneous local press and recipients’ testimony.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The CIA report infers that the Revolution Council was part of a prior plan rather than an improvised response, using the decree’s reported preparation/signature and broadcast sequence.
claim_type: CIA analytical inference from retrospective testimony and event chronology
confidence: High that the report argues this; moderate as an interpretation of the available chronology.
basis_and_limitations: CIA printed pp.25–27; Cornell’s reproduced decision and radio chronology are a separate source for public documents. The CIA conclusion does not identify who saw, approved or understood the decree before broadcast, and does not prove Politburo-wide authorization.
next_verification: Read the original signed decree, RRI transmission logs, signatories’ records, CDB messages and contemporaneous party minutes; align time stamps and document provenance.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The CIA report hypothesizes that Aidit probably drafted the PKI Political Bureau statement issued on 5 October because it resembled reported local instructions and a reported letter to East Java; it does not present a recovered draft.
claim_type: CIA authorship hypothesis about a public party statement
confidence: High that CIA makes the inference; low-to-moderate for actual authorship.
basis_and_limitations: CIA printed pp.79–80 says the evidence “suggests” Aidit drafted it. Cornell S115 reproduces the statement from newspaper texts and dates it 5 October; neither source supplies the draft, author’s copy, approval record or publication instruction.
next_verification: Find the Indonesian/Javanese newspaper originals, original party statement, drafts, dispatch/circulation instructions, and Aidit/Politburo correspondence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: ANRI’s 2024 Guide to Sukarno-era defense/security archives lists KOTI item 365 (Army newspaper clippings on G30S/Council, 1–11 October), item 366 (October 1965 chronology report) and item 369 (newspaper copies of the 1 October announcement received by the economic ministry).
claim_type: Official archival guide / multiple retrieval leads
confidence: High for the guide entries and locators; no conclusion yet about the folders’ contents.
basis_and_limitations: Printed p.116, Nos.365–366 and 369. The descriptions identify copies/printouts and one-sample folders; the underlying records were not opened. These leads are distinct from KOTI inventory item 515 (S228).
next_verification: Request all three folders and record original publication dates, source newspaper/RRI, copy marks, attachments and filing context; compare with item 515.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The public Political Bureau statement reproduced by Cornell is dated 5 October and its Indonesian/Javanese text is said to have appeared in Ariwarti Waspada on 8 and 9 October; Sudisman’s 1967 testimony refers to a Political Bureau statement dated 6 October; a later Unhas thesis cites another statement dated 10 October.
claim_type: Date and document-identity discrepancy across contemporary text and retrospective/secondary references
confidence: High that the sources report these dates; unresolved whether the 6 October reference is a date error or another text, and the 10 October text is separately reported but not authenticated.
basis_and_limitations: S115 provides the Oct. 5 document/date and newspaper publication dates; CIA S251 calls it issued Oct. 5; S260 says “dated October 6”; S679 reports a separate Oct. 10 statement. No Oct. 6 original or authenticated Oct. 10 original was obtained.
next_verification: Compare Ariwarti Waspada Oct. 6, 8–9 and Oct. 10 issues, identify separate Politburo releases, retrieve the IISH source cited in S679 and inspect Sudisman’s Indonesian trial transcript.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A 2024 Unhas thesis reproduces text attributed to a separate Political Bureau CC PKI statement dated 10 October 1965; it refers back to the 5 October statement and Sukarno’s 6 October cabinet message and urges calm, unity and resistance to provocation.
period: 1965-10-10; local Makassar response later in October
claim_type: Secondary transcription of a claimed contemporary party statement
confidence: Moderate that the thesis transcribes a distinct text and cites an IISH source; low-to-moderate for exact wording/date until the original is read.
basis_and_limitations: Printed p.42 and footnote 33 of the thesis cite IISG via an obsolete prog-ind.net URL. The old page was inaccessible; IISH’s guide identifies a 261-microfiche PKI documents/serials collection but no item-level record for this statement.
next_verification: Search the current IISH catalogue under PKI documents/serials, request microfiche/scans for Oct. 10 statement, identify its publication and compare with the thesis transcription.

atomic_claim_or_observation: In his July 1967 defense, Sudisman says he personally agreed with the officers’ action and was individually involved; he says he expected their Revolutionary Council to work with Sukarno to defend the left government’s anti-imperialist and limited anti-landlord policies.
period: 1965 events as recalled at the 1967 trial
claim_type: Detained participant’s retrospective self-attribution and political rationale
confidence: High that the published defense records this position; moderate-to-low as a complete contemporaneous account.
basis_and_limitations: The testimony places Sudisman’s personal stance alongside claims that the Central Committee as a whole had not adopted a formal decision. He was a detained defendant, prepared the speech from memory, and lacked the original meeting record. Individual assent must not be converted into proof of a unanimous Politburo or whole-party resolution.
next_verification: Compare original Indonesian transcript/audio, other defendants’ testimony, Politburo/Secretariat minutes, Aidit’s Oct. 6 letter, and local CDB records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Sudisman’s 1967 analysis attributes failure partly to subjectivism, failure to calculate the balance of forces and choose timing/leadership effectively, and isolation from any mass upsurge; he also criticizes political and organizational errors including weak internal criticism, liberalism and commandism.
period: PKI strategy through the 1965 defeat; written in 1967
confidence: High that the 1967 defense and 1966 self-criticism contain these diagnoses; moderate as an exhaustive causal account.
basis_and_limitations: Sudisman’s trial speech and the September 1966 Politburo self-criticism are situated post-defeat documents produced under repression and ideological realignment. They identify internal explanations but cannot alone establish the relative weight of military capacity, repression, foreign assistance, class conflict or local conditions.
next_verification: Compare the 1966 Indonesian text, leadership drafts/dissent, county-level party records, military capacity and repression orders, mass-organization records, and Southeast Asian party comparisons.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Sudisman says he prepared his analysis after more than seven months in detention, 14 interrogations over 18 days totaling at least 70 hours, more than 40 preliminary interrogations, and without books or a library, relying on memory.
claim_type: Testimony about detention and statement-production conditions
confidence: High that Sudisman’s published text states these conditions; the underlying interrogation logs and cell records remain unverified.
basis_and_limitations: Opening of the 21 July 1967 defense speech. His statement is direct testimony about his experience but has not been checked against detention/interrogation records; this caveat limits how the speech is used as an account of earlier decisions.
next_verification: Obtain Mahmilub transcript, interrogation schedules and records, prison medical/visitation log, counsel files and the 1975 Indonesian/English publication history.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hilmar Farid’s 2008 discussion of John Roosa argues that G30S leaders lacked a common view and a clear contingency plan after failure, distinguishes the movement from the subsequent mass killings, and identifies the order to kill the generals as unresolved.
confidence: High that Farid advances this argument; it is not independent corroboration of the underlying events.
basis_and_limitations: The essay is a book discussion based on Roosa and participant materials; it makes a useful research distinction but does not replace original records or settle who knew, ordered or carried out each act.
next_verification: Read the specific documents Roosa and Farid rely on, then compare Supardjo, Subekti, Sudisman, trial files, radio/Army records and death-scene evidence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: In André Liem’s published interview chapter, Rewang says the PKI as an institution did not decide to launch G30S; he recalls roughly ten Politburo members as confused afterward, says the party hoped Sukarno would restrain the Army, and places any Aidit involvement outside a formal Politburo decision.
claim_type: Retrospective participant testimony reproduced in oral-history scholarship
confidence: High that the chapter records these statements; low-to-moderate as a complete account of who knew or authorized what.
basis_and_limitations: Rewang says he joined the Politburo in mid-1965. This is his retrospective account in a 2004 chapter based on interviews, not Politburo minutes. It does not negate Sudisman’s separate claim of personal agreement/participation or CIA’s interrogation-derived account of limited briefings.
next_verification: Compare with Sudisman’s full Indonesian defense, CIA interrogation files, dated Politburo/Secretariat records, provincial CDB statements and RRI logs; distinguish institution-wide authorization from individual knowledge.

atomic_claim_or_observation: After Sudisman’s arrest in December 1966, Rewang says he proposed that surviving leaders leave Jakarta, organize resistance from rural areas, and move to a base; he recalls that the proposal was accepted and that East Java CDB contacts had prepared villages.
claim_type: Retrospective participant testimony in oral-history scholarship
confidence: High that Rewang’s proposal and acceptance are recorded in the interview; moderate for the decision sequence; exact date and implementing roster remain unverified.
basis_and_limitations: Liem records the interview rather than contemporaneous orders. Later reports give different dates for arrival, base preparation and Kompro formation; do not collapse those events into one move.
next_verification: Obtain Rewang memoir pages, travel/identity records, CDB correspondence, village contact records and captured committee papers.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The South Blitar organization is described as a layered emergency structure: an Emergency CC above provincial leadership and base-project committees (Kompro); Rewang recalls about nine CC members and says formation of guerrilla detachments had begun, while a participant describes the network as compartmentalized.
period: 1966–1968; South Blitar and other planned bases
confidence: High that interviewees describe these layers; moderate for the precise roster, scope and operational effectiveness.
basis_and_limitations: The article says names and reporting lines were deliberately restricted and that interviewees did not know the full Kompro roster. “Detachments begun” does not mean a completed or combat-capable army.
next_verification: Find Emergency CC and CDB minutes, appointment circulars, Kompro rosters, captured papers, orders, communications and unit/personnel records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Rewang says the leadership had not fixed a start date for organized people’s war and was waiting for a national conference to assess political conditions and organizational readiness; the planned conference had not yet occurred.
confidence: High that Rewang makes this claim; moderate about how consistently it governed dispersed networks.
basis_and_limitations: No national conference resolution, attendance list or authenticated directive has been obtained. The memoir-derived May 23, 1967 Emergency CC date is not confirmed by Liem’s interview chapter.
next_verification: Find the proposed conference notice, CDB delegate lists, cancellation/postponement records, and all surviving instructions on when armed struggle could begin.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Rewang describes local acts including disarming plantation guards and attacking people he called past “executioners” as acts outside the Kompro/CC program; he retrospectively calls some “armed propaganda,” while also acknowledging that they constituted armed action in a concrete sense.
claim_type: Retrospective participant interpretation of local operations
confidence: High that the chapter records this distinction; low-to-moderate as a complete inventory of actions and authorization across all cells.
basis_and_limitations: Rewang distinguishes a formal, organized people’s war—which still awaited preparation and a national conference—from concrete local military acts already occurring. His “armed propaganda” phrase does not erase the actions or their consequences. No dated action order, complete target/perpetrator list or independent record identifies every incident; this is a participant’s retrospective assessment.
next_verification: Identify each reported disarmament, guard-post incident and attack from local police/Army logs, village testimony, detainee files and party correspondence; compare dates and chain of command.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A Muyatno interview in Liem’s chapter identifies “Gatot Taryo” as the contact who introduced him to the South Blitar Kompro and describes him as its chair; Muyatno says he could identify few others because contacts were compartmentalized.
confidence: High that the interview transcript reports this; moderate for the individual’s role; no independent appointment record found.
basis_and_limitations: The name form “Gatot Taryo” should not be silently equated with similarly named figures in other sources. The witness explicitly says he did not know the full roster.
next_verification: Compare name variants against Rewang memoir, military capture/interrogation records, local civil identity files and Kompro documents.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A later article citing Rewang’s memoir dates the Emergency CC’s formation to 1967-05-23; Liem’s earlier interview chapter describes its structure and decisions but does not supply that exact date.
period: 1967-05-23; date of Emergency CC formation claimed retrospectively
claim_type: Secondary report citing a participant memoir, cross-checked against an oral-history chapter
confidence: High that the later article prints this date; low-to-moderate for the exact date until the cited memoir page or a contemporaneous record is inspected.
basis_and_limitations: Several later reports may depend on the same Rewang memoir and do not constitute independent confirmation. Liem’s non-dating is not proof against May 23.
next_verification: Read Rewang memoir at the cited pages and look for meeting minutes, dated appointment notices, letters and participant calendars.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Published accounts disagree on the date of the Communist Party of Thailand’s first armed clash: Cui Feng (citing a Thai military history) and a northeastern village study give 7 August 1965, while Ian Baird’s 2025 article gives 8 August. The exact date remains unresolved; neither date alone establishes the insurgency’s scale or readiness.
claim_type: Secondary historical account citing a 1986 Thai military history
confidence: High that the reviewed publications differ; moderate on the incident date pending direct comparison of the underlying Thai military records and local chronology.
basis_and_limitations: Cui Feng’s 2022 article cites Saiyud 1986 p.180; the village case study identifies the date through local oral history/commemoration; Baird’s 2025 article cites other secondary histories. None of the cited 1965 incident reports was inspected.
next_verification: Retrieve Saiyud 1986 p.180, the village study’s underlying interviews, Thai security incident reports and CPT records; determine whether 7/8 August refers to different locations or event stages.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A 1968 U.S. National Intelligence Estimate contrasted a few hundred PKI activists in Central/East Java trying to build a guerrilla force with a Malayan Communist Party force estimated below 1,000 at the Thai border, about 500 Sarawak guerrillas, roughly 150 armed Huks, and a roughly 4,000-member Burma Communist Party/White Flag insurgency; it described Laos as territorially distinct and dependent on North Vietnamese forces.
claim_type: Contemporary U.S. intelligence snapshot, not a comparable force census
confidence: High that the estimate uses these categories and numbers; low-to-moderate for comparability and actual strength.
basis_and_limitations: The estimates differ in date, definition and source quality; the NIE uses Cold War language and sometimes infers external direction without disclosed evidence. Huk estimates also differ across U.S. documents (about 140 in a 1967 note versus about 150 in the 1968 NIE).
next_verification: Build separate profiles using each party’s records, state incident files, territorial control, trained combatant vs sympathizer definitions and dated local rosters.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Cui Feng’s article describes a distinct regional foreign-support channel: U.S./Thai assistance to KMT forces on the Burma–Thailand frontier in the early 1950s, followed by Thai state use of remaining KMT units in northern border operations against the CPT from late 1969.
claim_type: Peer-reviewed secondary reconstruction of regional Cold War military channels
confidence: High that the article describes the channel; moderate for the underlying transfers because the article relies on earlier scholarship and did not expose the original CIA/Thai logistics files.
basis_and_limitations: This is outside Indonesia and must not be used as evidence for U.S. support to the Indonesian Army or for U.S. involvement in G30S. The late-1969 Thai arrangement followed a different state/foreign-force mechanism.
next_verification: Inspect cited CIA, Thai police and ROC records; compare arms approval, transfer, receipt, deployment and payment stages.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The available evidence differentiates three Indonesian forms of militarization: a public Fifth Force proposal and limited, partly unverified civilian training; the Indonesian Army’s established territorial command and local auxiliary structures; and the post-1966 PKI’s small, compartmentalized underground cells and planned guerrilla detachments. They are not equivalent forces.
confidence: Moderate-high as a distinction across the sources; exact coverage and strength of each form remain incomplete.
basis_and_limitations: A proposal is not a formed force; a training file title is not attendance or arms receipt; an Army territorial command is not proof of uniform local execution; a planned underground detachment is not proof of an operational army.
next_verification: Compare provincial military rosters/orders and civilian training attendance with PKI unit lists, budgets, weapons evidence, commands and action reports.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana reports that a 13 October 1965 order established Pupelrada at Korem 083 in Malang under Colonel Sumadi, extending Pepelrada coordination to the Korem/regency level; the article says the framework carried powers to restrict movement and detain people for up to 30 days.
claim_type: Scholarly transcription and interpretation of contemporaneous regional command records
confidence: High that the article identifies the order and describes these powers; moderate for the exact legal scope and local use until the original decree is reviewed.
basis_and_limitations: Leksana cites Pepelrada decree Kep-15/10/65 and an October 16 radiogram. No signed original, complete legal text, appeal record, or local order was opened. The legal powers cannot be assumed to have been exercised identically across districts.
next_verification: Obtain Kep-15/10/65, district Pupelrada installation orders, detention registers, travel restrictions, review/appeal files, and local reports.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana reports a 6 November 1965 radiogram ordering Puterpra units to be armed, including assignment of a Technical Assistance Unit to weaker units.
claim_type: Scholarly quotation of a regional military radiogram
confidence: High that the article quotes this instruction; low-to-moderate for arms actually issued, unit strength, and combat use.
basis_and_limitations: The original is cited as Radiogram T. 658/1965 to Kodim 0818–0825 and 0831. An arming order establishes planned authorization, not serial-numbered weapons delivery or use.
next_verification: Inspect T. 658/1965, arms receipts and returns, Puterpra/Technical Assistance Unit rosters, training logs, and operations reports.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana reports that a 27 November 1965 radiogram ordered mass movements to cease, routed the ambiguously labeled civilian group AA through Hansip, provided uniforms, and placed the movements under Army direction.
claim_type: Scholarly quotation of a regional military radiogram
confidence: High that the article reports this order; moderate for date and serial until the underlying record is checked.
basis_and_limitations: The 2020 article and Leksana’s 2023 monograph repeat T.702/1965 for both the 23 and 27 November instructions. This confirms the persistent printed citation, not the original serial/date; the two publications draw on the same inventory 316-a and are not independent confirmation.
next_verification: Read both original radiograms and the archive checklist; verify serial, dispatch date, recipients, definition of AA, uniforms issued, and local implementation.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hammer reports that a 26 October 1965 meeting in Solo chaired by Sarwo Edhie decided to involve pre-existing anti-communist village guards and augment them with newly recruited formations; RPKAD provided brief training to the new auxiliaries.
claim_type: Regional scholarly reconstruction citing military history and field interviews
confidence: High that Hammer reports the decision and training; moderate for exact implementation by district.
basis_and_limitations: The 26 October meeting is cited through the 1971 Diponegoro military history and Jenkins/Kammen; training duration, personnel, attendance, weapons and individual unit conduct are not established by the order alone. This is Central Java evidence, not a national template.
next_verification: Obtain the 26 October meeting minutes, village-guard rosters, new auxiliary recruitment lists, RPKAD training reports, weapons receipts, and district deployment logs.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana’s East Java evidence shows a shift in the stated task from early public-order management to organized anti-left coordination: an 11 October instruction tasked Zeni Battalion 5 with assisting Puterpra to control demonstrations and prevent property destruction, while the later 21 October Pancasila Operation directed operations against communists and allowed pro-Army civilians to assist.
claim_type: Scholarly reconstruction from quoted military records
confidence: High for the different stated purposes in the cited instructions; moderate for how consistently the shift was implemented.
basis_and_limitations: The 11 October order is Radiogram T. 582/1965; the 21 October order is Perintah Operasi No. 5 Pantja Sila. Early local violence and anti-left civilian organization were already present; changing orders do not mean every earlier incident was non-political or that every later locality followed the same sequence.
next_verification: Read both signed orders, event logs before and after 21 October, recipient-unit records, and district reports to map timing and divergence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana’s account attributes East Java’s delayed provincial command action partly to political realignment and troop shortages: it reports that eight of sixteen provincial battalions were deployed elsewhere, cites a report that roughly 30 percent had been implicated in G30S, and relays a U.S.-intelligence-based claim that Basuki Rachmat said he had sufficient forces to continue the purge only by 19 November.
claim_type: Scholar’s synthesis of retrospective military studies, an intelligence-officer report, and a dissertation’s U.S. cable citation
confidence: High that Leksana presents these constraints and cites this source chain; moderate-to-low for exact manpower and for the causal weight assigned to it.
basis_and_limitations: The battalion figures are transmitted through Anderson/Robinson and the 19 November claim through Setiyawan’s use of U.S. intelligence, not through original rosters or the cable inspected here. Political hesitation, troop availability and alliance formation may interact; the evidence does not reduce the delay to one cause.
next_verification: Obtain 1965 Brawijaya battalion rosters and movement orders, the 29 November East Java report, the cited U.S. cable, and Basuki Rachmat/Colonel Widjaja Sukardanu correspondence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The Amnesty International Indonesia 1965 document archive has an ethnicity-of-victim taxonomy, but states that its document collection concerning the 1965 tragedy covers 1967–2016; the Chinese, Dayak, Javanese and other tags are document-retrieval categories, not a 1965–66 victim-level death register.
claim_type: Directly inspected archive metadata and category pages
confidence: High for the archive’s stated scope and indexing design.
basis_and_limitations: The site says it contains more than 200 public PDFs and avoids an individual-name search. A document carrying an ethnicity tag may discuss later detention, court cases, discrimination or historical context; tag presence does not enumerate deaths or establish that a particular tagged person was killed.
next_verification: Use the archive to locate Amnesty reports and then extract dated individual cases only where the PDF supports them; do not aggregate category results as victim counts or ethnic shares.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana reports that Brawijaya Commander Basuki Rachmat and Pepelrada chief of staff Widjaja Sukardanu were considered hesitant to launch large-scale operations, amid a divided East Java political environment and troop shortage; she notes that anti-communism and personal Sukarno loyalty were not mutually exclusive among Brawijaya officers.
claim_type: Secondary military-political interpretation based on earlier scholarship and regional reports
confidence: High that the article advances this interpretation; moderate for individual motives and causal explanation.
basis_and_limitations: The underlying November 1965 intelligence-officer report and cited command rosters were not independently read. “Sukarnoist” describes reported political loyalty, not proof of support for the PKI or opposition to anti-communist action.
next_verification: Read the full 29 November East Java report, officers’ service and posting records, command minutes, troop movement logs and correspondence with Jakarta.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana reproduces a Korem 083/Kopur Siaga III detention log with reported totals of 2,472 detainees on 4 November 1965, 6,259 by noon on 12 December, 5,798 by midnight that day, and 4,431 on 29 December; the table separates military personnel, civilians in the armed forces, and public civilians on some dates.
claim_type: Scholarly transcription of a contemporaneous military detention log
confidence: High that Leksana’s publications reproduce these totals; moderate-to-low for the underlying register counts and their completeness until the original log is checked.
basis_and_limitations: The totals are detainees present at listed reporting times, not cumulative arrests, deaths, or a victim count. The original counting method and transfers, releases, deaths, duplicate registrations and subdistrict coverage are unspecified. S295 and S1410 are the same researcher and archive chain.
next_verification: Inspect the original Laporan G30S/PKI di Daerah Kopur Siaga III/83 Malang-Besuki pp.8–18, daily intake/outflow registers, Kodim returns, prisoner transfers and death records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The published Korem 083 detention table has major internal anomalies: it prints 1,509 detainees on 23 November between 4,020 on 21 November and 5,006 on 27 November, and leaves total fields blank for 4 and 23 December even though the component columns sum to 5,542 and 5,617 respectively.
claim_type: Direct audit of a scholarly transcription of a military table
confidence: High for the table as published; unknown whether the anomaly belongs to the military original, the archive copy, transcription, or table layout.
basis_and_limitations: The 2023 book repeats the same table drawn from inventory 316-a. A sharp entry change cannot be interpreted as mass release, killing, transfer, or reclassification without the original daily report and count definitions.
next_verification: Compare the scan page-by-page with the original archive table; inspect 21–28 November entries, totals and date headers; reconcile unit returns and transfers.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana reports that a 30 November 1965 radiogram required PKI-linked political or mass organizations’ claimed self-dissolution to be accepted by the Dandim as head of Pupelrada and witnessed by Panca Tunggal and National Front organizations.
claim_type: Scholarly quotation of a regional military radiogram
confidence: High that both versions of Leksana’s study report the clause; moderate for exact implementation and political pressure in each organization.
basis_and_limitations: This procedure places acceptance under a district military commander, complicating any unqualified description of organizational dissolution as voluntary. Both publications rely on the same Brawijaya archive record; the original T.715/1965 was not examined.
next_verification: Read T.715/1965, dissolution letters and meeting minutes; identify the Dandim, witnesses, organizations, dates, and whether leaders were coerced or detained.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A Korem 083 report cited by Leksana records four killing cases on 16 November 1965, including one event in which four bodies were found in a rice field; the report’s late-October-to-December language often names the dead but leaves the killers unidentified.
claim_type: Contemporaneous military reporting as transcribed by a historian
confidence: High that the historian reports these entries; moderate for the underlying incident details pending the original report and individual identifications.
basis_and_limitations: “Unidentified killer” is the report’s wording, not evidence that investigators did not know or that the killers were civilians. No victim names, autopsies, burial records or incident investigations were reviewed.
next_verification: Inspect inventory 316-a daily pages, police/civil death reports, cemetery and family records, and compare the 16 November entries against detention/transfer records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana reports that a 4 December 1965 Korem 083 report told the Brawijaya commander that PKI in the Korem 083 area had been “terminated”; this is a military status assertion, not a count of people killed.
claim_type: Contemporaneous military report quoted in a later study
confidence: High that the report contains this characterization as quoted; low as a literal description of every person or cell in the area.
basis_and_limitations: The same historical record includes thousands detained and local operations continuing after the command claim. “Terminated” may refer to organization, operational resistance, or an official narrative; it cannot be translated automatically into deaths.
next_verification: Read the report’s original Indonesian sentence and context, distribution chain, supporting unit returns, detention rolls, and January 1966 operation reports.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A 1966 South Malang military report, as cited by Leksana, identifies a local Pancasila Operation under P.O.004/1965 dated 19 November 1965, begun on 29 November and continuing to 18 January 1966: troops linked with Tjatur Tunggal and village heads in Donomulyo; Army raider units, Puterpra, Marines and Brimob operated in successive areas, with Brimob also guarding detainees.
period: 1965-11-19 to 1966-01-18; South Malang and Wates, Blitar
claim_type: Later scholar’s reconstruction from an identified contemporaneous military operation report and a 2019 interview
confidence: High that the cited report and interview are described this way; moderate for the sequence and unit assignments pending the original report and daily logs.
basis_and_limitations: The South Malang operation began more than five weeks after the province-wide Pancasila Operation order of 21 October. The report was produced by the operating command; its labels, chronology and self-presentation need comparison with village testimony, arrest registers and incident records.
next_verification: Obtain the 1966 Laporan Singkat Selama Operasi Pantjasila Malang Selatan, P.O.004/1965, daily orders, task force rosters, Donomulyo Koramil records, detention-site logs and local death/family records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The South Malang military report claimed that 90 percent of Donomulyo residents were PKI and that twelve firearms were found in western Donomulyo; it also described 24 remaining PKI/PR/BTI/Lekra activists for screening and used the term diselesaikan, translated in Leksana’s text as “terminated.”
claim_type: Military operational report quoted by a historian
confidence: High that the official report is quoted this way; low for the alleged 90 percent, the weapon-discovery context and what “diselesaikan” meant in each case.
basis_and_limitations: The 90-percent figure is a military allegation, not a population survey or measured party-membership rate. The report presents itself as restoring order and is addressed to superiors; “secured,” “screened,” “disbanded” and “terminated” require original-language/context review and survivor comparison.
next_verification: Inspect original P.O.004 operation report and screening lists; identify the 24 persons, legal/physical outcomes, firearm provenance, village denominator and whether “diselesaikan” meant processing, expulsion, detention or killing.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Jono, a local guard and former Catholic Youth/PMKRI activist interviewed in Donomulyo in 2016, told Leksana that detainees were taken from police custody to a public cemetery, tied and shot; he said the Army carried out killings and Ansor members sometimes assisted or killed.
period: 1965 operations remembered in a 2016 interview; Donomulyo, South Malang
claim_type: Retrospective eyewitness testimony reproduced in scholarly research
confidence: High that the published chapter records this testimony; moderate for the described incidents pending other eyewitness, burial and family corroboration.
basis_and_limitations: This is one local witness’s account, not a complete incident list or region-wide description. The interview recording/transcript and precise victim identities were not accessed. In the same passage, the military report frames events as “security” and the historian notes that official narrative underreports killings.
next_verification: Seek the full interview and consent/anonymity conditions, identify cemetery graves and named victims, locate other guards, families, detainees and Ansor/Army participants, and compare operation reports.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana’s monograph describes a July–September 1967 Brawijaya “New Orderisation” apparatus: Java Army commanders, Kostrad and RPKAD met in July; a provincial guidance team was authorized in September with military, action-front, mass/political-organization, Golkar, civil-service and press members; Korem/Kodim teams followed the territorial command chain, replaced village heads with Army caretakers in former PKI areas and postponed village elections.
claim_type: Scholar’s reconstruction from Brawijaya records and earlier military-political studies
confidence: High that the chapter reports the cited meeting, order and measures; moderate for province-wide execution and duration.
basis_and_limitations: Underlying Siaran Kilat No.1/1967, Kep-001/ORBA/9/1967 and team procedure annex in inventory 316-b were not inspected. The source’s claim about village-head replacement/election postponement needs district appointment lists and local election files.
next_verification: Obtain inventory 316-b order originals, July meeting participants/records, September guidance-team structure and work plans, caretaker appointment lists and postponed election registers.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Leksana reports that Radiogram T.587/1965, dated 14 October 1965, directed Kodim to work with local police and Panca Tunggal in investigating Gerwani and Pemuda Rakyat members about Jakarta volunteer training and their knowledge or implementation of G30S in their regions.
claim_type: Scholar’s transcription of a contemporaneous military order
confidence: High that the publications report this instruction; moderate pending the original radiogram and its implementation records.
basis_and_limitations: Leksana says the investigation concerned organizational knowledge/training, but whether this order directly affected killings is unclear. The 2020 paper and 2023 chapter share the same author and Brawijaya archive chain.
next_verification: Obtain T.587/1965 and attached Kodim replies; identify interrogated people, procedures, detention outcomes and links, if any, to later arrests or killings.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman’s reconstruction distinguishes post-1965 leadership positions: the Bandung group around Ismail Bakri, supported by Rewang, criticized the earlier legal-parliamentary strategy and reliance on Sukarno; the Jakarta group around Sudisman remained closer to Aidit’s line, although Sudisman later supported the September 1966 Politburo self-criticism.
claim_type: Scholarly reconstruction citing participant testimony and Imam Soedjono’s later memoir
confidence: Moderate that Hearman reports this distinction; low-to-moderate as a complete map of all factions or their changing membership.
basis_and_limitations: The factional interpretation is partly sourced through Soedjono’s 2006 memoir as cited in Hearman’s footnote; it is not based on contemporaneous group minutes. Do not treat either cluster as a fully coherent command chain.
next_verification: Read Soedjono’s cited pages and Sudisman’s 1966 self-criticism in Indonesian; seek Ismail Bakri/Rewang correspondence, the Jakarta group’s communications and regional committee records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Melvin’s summary of two 14 October 1965 South Aceh military-chronology entries reports four Chinese victims among five deaths at Blang Pidie (80%) and four Chinese victims among ten deaths at Sama Dua (40%). The article says the four named Chinese victims in the Sama Dua entry were all from Blang Pidie.
period: 1965-10-14; Blang Pidie and Sama Dua, South Aceh
claim_type: Event-level ratios calculated from a historian’s transcription of a military chronology
confidence: High for the printed counts and arithmetic; low for unique-person accounting and underlying event completeness until the original chronology is checked.
basis_and_limitations: The article calls these separate events but assigns the four named Sama Dua victims to Blang Pidie; residence/origin, event location and possible duplicate listing are not resolved here. Do not add the two rows into a 15-person victim total or call these ratios a district, provincial or national ethnic share.
next_verification: Inspect Chronologis 1966 p.8 image and full Indonesian wording; determine whether “from Blang Pidie” means residence, origin or attack location; match names, deaths, belongings, burial and family records across both entries.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Woolgar’s regional comparison reports that West Java saw Chinese association property attacks and Baperki arrests, but Chinese deaths were rare among the several thousand killings there; it contrasts this with harsher anti-communist/anti-Chinese conditions under northern Sumatra and Aceh commanders, including massacres, detention and forced expulsion. It also describes a broader state crackdown on Chinese organizations and property after March–May 1966.
period: 1965-10 to 1967; West Java, North Sumatra and Aceh
confidence: High that Woolgar reports these distinctions; moderate for province-wide comparison because casualty counts and enforcement records are incomplete and regionally non-equivalent.
basis_and_limitations: This does not provide comparable regional ethnic denominators or establish a national ethnic-victim percentage. Property destruction, detention, murder, organizational closure and expulsion must remain separate outcome fields. Woolgar’s national “not overrepresented” inference depends on approximate 2,000 and 500,000 estimates.
next_verification: Trace the article’s local press, command orders and citations; seek district-level Chinese/Baperki victim, detention, property and expulsion lists for West Java, Medan and Aceh with a common time window.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman reports that when Brawijaya units said local Hansip were passing information about military movements, the Army replaced those guards with Banser members and planned a larger Trisula operation.
confidence: High that Hearman reports this sequence; moderate-to-low for the asserted information leakage and its causal weight pending the underlying operation file.
basis_and_limitations: The claim of leakage appears in a military account, while the described replacement is reconstructed by Hearman from military and participant sources. The source does not establish that all Hansip cooperated with PKI or that every Banser member was under identical command.
next_verification: Inspect Operasi Trisula pp.167 and related orders, guard rosters, intelligence reports and interviews with displaced Hansip, Banser members and village residents.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hearman describes Trisula’s village-control system as replacing local administrators with caretakers (often military), stationing a company in each battalion-assigned village, checking identity and registering residents and cattle, placing checkpoints roughly 300–400 metres apart, and requiring military permission for public gatherings.
claim_type: Historical reconstruction from the Army’s Trisula history and local oral histories
confidence: High that the published study reports these methods; moderate for their exact coverage and village-by-village execution.
basis_and_limitations: These are counterinsurgency and territorial-control measures, not a casualty count. The underlying military history and complete village registers were not independently inspected; oral accounts and military self-report have different vantage points.
next_verification: Obtain Operasi Trisula pp.67, 85 and relevant appendices; compare village caretaker appointments, resident/cattle registers, checkpoint maps, movement permits and family testimony.

atomic_claim_or_observation: CiNii identifies Pauker’s 1969 RM-5753-PR as prepared for U.S. Air Force Project RAND under contract F44620-67-C-0045. The report is now directly read: pp.61–62 present Pauker’s account of disagreement over rebuilding a mass underground before armed struggle versus isolated actions; p.62 also gives his casualty/fate claims. Hearman separately reconstructs the domestic debate through interviews and military histories.
period: 1969 report analyzing post-1965 PKI; South Blitar debate 1967–1968
claim_type: Official library catalog metadata plus a later scholar’s quotation of a contemporaneous U.S.-sponsored analysis
confidence: High for the report’s text, title, sponsorship and contract; low-to-moderate for Pauker’s accuracy about covert PKI deliberations because he provides no source at the point of the strategic dispute and his Rewang death claim is demonstrably wrong.
basis_and_limitations: The official RAND scan (S1358) was opened and printed pp.61–62 visually checked on 2026-11-19. Hearman’s Rewang interview and TAPOL/Amnesty prison reporting independently establish survival. RAND sponsorship identifies an analytical channel, not direct evidence that the U.S. operated or collected through a particular covert mechanism.
next_verification: Compare the report’s sources/distribution file with emergency-CC minutes, Rewang and Munir accounts, army-history pages, court records and local incident evidence; recover original NYT sources behind its death estimate.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Lyon reports that Army Air Command pilot Sudjai recalled being entrusted from 1 October 1965 with personally delivering Suharto’s confidential orders and information to commanders of the three Java military divisions, requiring repeated flights between Jakarta and division headquarters.
claim_type: Retrospective participant memoir mediated by a later specialist article
confidence: High that Lyon reports this and quotes the memoir; moderate for the deliveries and contents because the five memoir installments and flight records were not retrieved.
basis_and_limitations: Lyon, “Testimony of a messenger,” “A pilot’s testimony” and “Plans for the destruction of the PKI”; source identified as Sudjai’s 2009 five-part memoir.
next_verification: Retrieve all five 2009 installments and compare Army Air Command logs, dispatches, receipts and regional command diaries.

atomic_claim_or_observation: In Sudjai’s account as summarized by Lyon, Java division commanders were initially uncertain and did not know one another’s responses; their dilemma joined hostility to the PKI with loyalty to Sukarno. Sudjai says all three accepted Suharto’s confidential demands by the third week of October.
claim_type: Retrospective participant account and later secondary interpretation
confidence: High that the article attributes this to Sudjai; moderate-to-low for exact sequence, private motives and timing pending original memoir and command records.
basis_and_limitations: Lyon, “Commanders’ uncertainty”; includes Sudjai’s recollection of Adji’s repeated fear of arrest, dismissal or demotion. Not a contemporary meeting minute.
next_verification: Identify all three commanders and obtain diaries, orders, meeting calendars, personnel records and dated operational directives.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Lyon says Sudjai recounted a rumor that Suharto permitted West Java commander Adji to maintain good relations with Sukarno as part of an understanding preceding Adji’s agreement to the anti-PKI campaign in West Java.
claim_type: Participant memoir reporting a rumor, mediated by a later article
confidence: High that Lyon reports the rumor; low for an actual bargain because the memoir itself presents it as rumor and no agreement record is cited.
basis_and_limitations: Lyon, “Commanders’ uncertainty.” Do not describe this as a documented agreement or direct proof of Sukarno’s role.
next_verification: Find Adji/Suharto correspondence, Siliwangi orders, meeting records and independent participant testimony.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Lyon interprets the confidential instructions carried by Sudjai as containing a plan to destroy the PKI down to local levels and foreshadowing an effort to implicate Sukarno; the public line of support for Sukarno and private instructions reportedly differed.
claim_type: Later author’s interpretation of a participant memoir
confidence: High that Lyon makes this interpretation; low-to-moderate as a conclusion about the orders because the orders and full memoir were not inspected.
basis_and_limitations: Lyon, “Plans for the destruction of the PKI”; underlying confidential orders are not reproduced in the article.
next_verification: Obtain original order texts and recipients’ copies; compare public speech transcript, Sukarno’s orders and regional operational directives.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Lyon reports that Sudjai’s memoir describes opportunities for overseas flight training at U.S. Army and U.S. Air Force flight schools in 1960.
claim_type: Retrospective memoir detail reported by a later specialist article
confidence: High that the article states this; low-to-moderate for exact program, attendance and financing because memoir and training records were not retrieved.
basis_and_limitations: Lyon, “A pilot’s testimony”; describes training opportunities, not a documented covert mission or complete aid-program record.
next_verification: Search U.S. Army/Air Force foreign training rosters, grant/travel records, Indonesian Army personnel files and Sudjai’s service record.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Lyon reports Sudjai’s account that the Indonesian Army rushed an order in 1964 for two U.S.-manufactured twin-engine Aero Grand Commander aircraft to strengthen strike and command-and-control capability; Army pilots ferried them from the United States, with Sudjai arriving in Jakarta in late August 1964.
claim_type: Retrospective participant memoir reported by a later specialist article
confidence: High that the memoir as summarized says this; moderate for the purchase, delivery date and purpose until procurement and transfer records are checked.
basis_and_limitations: Lyon, “A pilot’s testimony”; no contract, payment, export-license, delivery or unit assignment document was examined. Procurement evidence is not proof of U.S. political action in 1965.
next_verification: Find Army procurement/budget files, U.S. export and sales records, aircraft serials, delivery documents, training records and 1965 flight logs.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Lyon reports that Sudjai recalled flying Suharto on secret night or pre-dawn flights in early October, including a pre-dawn 3 October trip to Semarang after loyalist forces retook it, and flying Suharto to Semarang again around Aidit’s capture in November.
claim_type: Retrospective participant memoir mediated by a later article
confidence: High that Lyon reports these recollections; moderate for exact dates and details pending memoir, logs and parallel records.
basis_and_limitations: Lyon, “Suharto’s pilot”; retrospective recollection does not establish the full operational purpose of each flight.
next_verification: Compare Army Air Command plans, Semarang command records, Aidit capture documentation and other crew/passenger testimony.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 6 October 1965 CIA memorandum says it had “reliably” been reported that the PKI in August reviewed contingency plans to be used if Sukarno died within the next days or weeks; it describes seclusion of senior leaders and protection of party assets by youth and security cadres. The cable gives no source or underlying document.
claim_type: Contemporaneous intelligence report of an unattributed report
confidence: High that the CIA memorandum records this report; low-to-moderate for the existence and exact content of the alleged contingency plan absent its source record.
basis_and_limitations: FRUS d149, para.16. The document says “reliably reported” but does not identify the source, meeting, author or written plan.
next_verification: Find the cited intelligence source, PKI Politburo/secretariat minutes, Aidit papers and contemporaneous participant records; distinguish succession contingency planning from authorization of 30 September operations.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The same CIA memorandum hypothesized that news of Sukarno’s apparent illness on the evening of 30 September, combined with partial or garbled knowledge of a contingency plan for his death, may have influenced the movement’s timing; it further guessed militants expected swift action and a new council to force Sukarno and the country to support them.
confidence: High that the CIA proposed this hypothesis; low for the underlying causal sequence because it is not tied to a named witness or operational document.
basis_and_limitations: FRUS d149, para.17 uses “plausible view,” “may have,” and “probably”; this is an analytic reconstruction, not a direct record of the planners’ thinking.
next_verification: Compare Sudisman, Subekti, Supardjo, Untung and Sjam accounts; locate Sukarno’s 30 September schedule/medical record, operation planning notes and communications about his illness.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 6 October CIA memorandum judged that Aidit probably did not approve killing the generals or changing the government, because the political situation appeared favorable to the PKI, while allowing that a few militant Central Committee members might have supported the plan.
confidence: High that the memo expresses this judgment; low-to-moderate as a conclusion about Aidit’s actual knowledge or approval because the memo identifies no direct evidence and describes its view as a probability.
basis_and_limitations: FRUS d149, para.18. This was an early assessment; compare later participant accounts without treating later trials as automatically more reliable.
next_verification: Compare original party records and testimony by Aidit’s aides, Sudisman, Subekti, Munir, Sjam and Supardjo; seek contemporaneous communications and calendars.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 6 October CIA memorandum reports that Sukarno’s 2 October broadcast said he had assumed personal command of the Army, appointed General Pranoto administrative head, and deputized Suharto to restore security; the memo says a 3 October KOTI broadcast described Pranoto only as “assisting” the president.
claim_type: Contemporaneous diplomatic/intelligence report of public statements
confidence: High that the CIA memo reports these broadcasts and wording; moderate for exact wording pending original Indonesian audio/transcripts. It records asserted formal authority, not proof of who controlled units in practice.
basis_and_limitations: FRUS d149, paras.6–7. The report also records Suharto’s statement affirming Sukarno’s changes; the underlying broadcasts were not directly inspected in this round.
next_verification: Retrieve RRI and KOTI transcripts/audio, presidential appointment/order, Army headquarters directives and regional receipt/implementation records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 6 October CIA memorandum reports that Sukarno rejected Army proposals for firm measures against the movement’s leaders and PKI on 4 October, describing the issue as political and asking generals to leave settlement to him; it says Army officers were depressed after the meeting.
claim_type: Contemporaneous intelligence report of a presidential meeting and attributed reactions
confidence: High that the memo records this account; moderate for the exact words and participant reactions until checked against Indonesian minutes, recordings and separate witnesses.
basis_and_limitations: FRUS d149, para.9. “Depressed” is the memorandum’s reported characterization, not a measured group response.
next_verification: Find the 4 October meeting attendee list, minutes, Sukarno speech/transcript, commanders’ diaries and orders issued immediately afterward.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The CIA memorandum assessed that Sukarno’s repeated broadcasts, together with pro-Sukarno/pro-Army positions attributed to Tjakrabirawa commander Sabur and Central Java commander Surjosumpeno, appeared to reduce Untung’s following; it also said reports of his remaining support varied from 110 troops to several battalions.
claim_type: Contemporaneous intelligence assessment with conflicting force estimates
confidence: High that the memo records this assessment and range; low-to-moderate for the amount of support lost because the report calls the information confused and does not explain its source or counting method.
basis_and_limitations: FRUS d149, para.4. The range itself warns against treating an early CIA count as a unit roster.
next_verification: Compare Central Java unit rolls, defections, radio logs, command reports and movement records; identify the sources behind each estimate.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Davidson and Kammen report that the banned West Kalimantan PKI maintained an urban underground during 1966 and early 1967, established a Singkawang city committee in April 1967, recruited in Pontianak and Sambas, and linked urban cadres to forest-based resistance and training sites.
claim_type: Peer-reviewed regional historical reconstruction drawing on military histories, press and interviews
confidence: High that the article reports this organizational sequence; moderate for its full extent and operational continuity because the underlying rosters, minutes and training registers were not examined.
basis_and_limitations: Davidson and Kammen, “Indonesia’s Unknown War,” pp.59–61; their footnotes cite a 1970 Kodam history and regional press.
next_verification: Find city committee membership, meeting records, training attendance, village contacts and captured internal correspondence; separate military press claims from participant evidence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Davidson and Kammen say West Kalimantan PKI leader Said Achmad Sofyan and followers left Pontianak for a forested base called Bukit Bara in late 1965 or possibly early 1966, located near rural Chinese communities and remaining coastal cadres.
claim_type: Regional scholarly reconstruction from military records, press and participant materials
confidence: Moderate that the relocation occurred; low-to-moderate for exact date and precise site because the authors themselves state the date is uncertain and Bara does not appear on available maps.
basis_and_limitations: Davidson and Kammen, pp.59–60 and notes 28–29; cited military manuscript and a 1967 Kompas map/report. Do not infer that residents of nearby Chinese communities were party members or combatants.
next_verification: Locate the cited unpublished military manuscript, the 1967 Kompas map/article, Sofyan interviews and village-level names/household records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Davidson and Kammen distinguish four origins in the West Kalimantan rebellion—Paraku, PGRS, Indonesian volunteers, and the banned provincial PKI—and describe a post-Konfrontasi convergence into two loose groupings: PGRS/Paraku oriented toward Sarawak, and PKI members with some former volunteers oriented toward West Kalimantan. They say the groups had contact but remained distinct through early 1967.
claim_type: Peer-reviewed historical synthesis and organizational distinction
confidence: High that the authors make this distinction; moderate for group boundaries and exact contacts, which were fluid and reconstructed from mixed sources.
basis_and_limitations: Davidson and Kammen, pp.57–60; see also existing C322/C673. The authors argue contemporaneous military and Western framing collapsed distinct groups into a single China-linked insurgency.
next_verification: Compare party and guerrilla rosters, PGRS/Paraku internal records, Indonesian military reports, Sarawak branch histories and border-crossing/interrogation records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: For April 1967, Davidson and Kammen report a meeting between Sofyan’s PKI group and PGRS/Paraku members to plan a joint offensive; they relay a military-history account that about thirty PGRS members left over a strategic dispute and joined Sofyan, while cautioning that the Army’s broad PGRS label could mean some were actually PKI members.
claim_type: Later scholarly reconstruction from military history and an unpublished military manuscript
confidence: High that the article reports the meeting and competing account; low-to-moderate for the thirty-person roster and its organizational identity because source attribution is contested and the underlying records are not open.
