confidence: High that Crouch reports this account; moderate-to-low for the signed order, intended number and exact scope until the cited Omar Dhani proceedings and AURI files are checked.
basis_and_limitations: Crouch, printed p.92 and note 71, cites Sri Muljono testimony in Omar Dhani trial vol.III p.489. The cited volume was not obtained. This reported base-Hansip instruction may be related to, but is not identical with, a Fifth Force decision or the later Lubang Buaya course.
next_verification: Obtain the Omar Dhani trial volume III pp.468–489, Sri Muljono’s signed/court statement, Halim staffing shortage records, the 120-person plan and base-defense orders.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Crouch reports that Sujono began training at Lubang Buaya on 5 July, usually ran two courses per month with 200–300 per group, and that a final September group rose to 1,200; this numerical summary must remain attributed to Crouch and must not be merged with Sujono’s separate courtroom statements of about 1,500 arrivals and an indirect “1,000-something” report.
period: 5 Jul–Sep 1965; reported in 1978/2007 and testimony in 1966
claim_type: Secondary summary compared with a witness’s courtroom account
confidence: High that Crouch gives these counts and cites the Njono trial; low-to-moderate for the cohort sizes and definitions without course lists or rechecking the original pages.
basis_and_limitations: Crouch printed p.92, note 73 cites Sujono at Njono trial pp.207, 214 and 225. The existing courtroom record excerpt distinguishes different information bases; no attendance roll or cohort schedule has been found. “1,200 last group,” “1,500 arrived” and the representative’s indirect “1,000-something” are not interchangeable totals.
next_verification: Compare the cited trial page images and complete transcript, then obtain course calendars, attendance rolls, transport and supply records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Crouch reports that Air Force deputy Ignatius Dewanto ordered the volunteer training stopped on 21 September 1965 after finding participants were predominantly from the Communist element of Nasakom, with future courses intended for nationalist and religious organizations; Crouch cites Dewanto’s testimony at Omar Dhani trial vol.III p.47.
claim_type: Secondary report of a military-court statement about command action
confidence: High that Crouch attributes this account to Dewanto; low-to-moderate that the order was issued and implemented as stated until the cited testimony and order are obtained.
basis_and_limitations: Crouch printed p.92, note 74. The Omar Dhani court volume and a written stop order were not inspected. The account does not establish all activity at the site ended on that date.
next_verification: Obtain vol.III p.47, any Dewanto testimony transcript and the 21 September written/coded order, recipient acknowledgements and the proposed 1 October course schedule.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Crouch reports a 21 September stop order but does not establish the date the course actually ceased. The 1994 State Secretariat transcription says training ran from 5 July until the September 30 Movement began; Ambarwulan and Kasdi (2012) report an early-September order and actual closure on 26 September, but the chapter’s nearby footnote to Soedarmanto p.106 follows the preceding “Bung So” sentence and is not clearly attached to the closure paragraph; Anderson and McVey date training to the eve of 1 October. The endpoints may refer to different courses, orders, actual classes, or use of the site; the issue remains unresolved.
claim_type: Unresolved timeline divergence across a historian’s synthesis and an official retrospective narrative
confidence: High that the four accounts differ in phrasing and date; low regarding the actual order, final class, participant activity or site closure.
basis_and_limitations: Crouch cites Dewanto’s Omar Dhani trial testimony vol.III p.47; that volume is unavailable. The official account is a third-party transcription. Ambarwulan/Kasdi’s surrounding subsection has a note to Soedarmanto p.106, but its scope is unclear; the page was not inspected. Anderson/McVey is an explicitly provisional reconstruction partly dependent on late-1965 press. “Order issued,” “class ended,” “training program ceased” and “site cleared” are distinct events.
next_verification: Obtain Omar Dhani trial III p.47 and any written stop order; inspect Soedarmanto p.106 and identify its scope, informant/document; locate daily course and site records, final attendance/return and weapons logs; compare the 1994 original and Anderson/McVey cited press.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Anderson and McVey’s 1971 interim report reconstructs a summer 1965 AURI–PKI arrangement for field training lower-level PKI cadres, with local PKI chiefs apparently selecting candidates and volunteers signing up on party instruction; it dates training from early July to the eve of 1 October.
period: Summer 1965; reconstruction prepared Jan 1966 and published 1971
claim_type: Early scholarly reconstruction based on press and post-event reporting
confidence: High that the report makes this reconstruction; moderate-to-low that it establishes a formal agreement or centrally authorized party decision.
basis_and_limitations: Printed pp.19–20 and notes 14, 29–31. The preface says the analysis was preliminary and was based on late-1965 metropolitan and provincial press. Training details partly rely on post-event newspaper “confessions”; these are not independent course or command records.
next_verification: Locate AURI/PKI correspondence, local party dispatches, trainee sign-up lists, full course roster and the newspaper reports/confessions cited in notes 14 and 29.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Anderson and McVey explain the AURI–PKI training relationship through institutional rivalry with the Army, the Air Force leadership’s alignment with Sukarno, and differing outlooks among senior and mid-level officers; they explicitly do not treat the Air Force as a politically uniform or simply PKI-ideological actor.
confidence: High that this is the report’s interpretation; not proof of individual officers’ private beliefs or a unitary Air Force policy.
basis_and_limitations: Printed pp.19–20. The report is an early, explicitly provisional reconstruction and relies heavily on contemporaneous press; compare with Crouch and trial records, noting citation overlap.
next_verification: Compare individual officers’ statements and personnel/command records with Army–AURI correspondence, service doctrine, contemporaneous press and full trial records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Ambarwulan and Aminuddin Kasdi’s 2012 chapter reports that Air Force deputy Dewanto convened an early-September meeting about Lubang Buaya training and ordered it closed; the authors state that the training was actually closed on 26 September 1965. A nearby note 63 to J. B. Soedarmanto’s 2004 biography of Harry Tjan Silalahi, p.106, follows the preceding “Bung So” sentence; it is unclear whether this note also supports the Dewanto/closure account.
claim_type: Retrospective secondary report and citation-chain observation
confidence: High that the 2012 chapter states these details; low-to-moderate for the meeting, order and actual closure until its evidentiary basis and dated course records are checked.
basis_and_limitations: Read printed pp.160–161 through third-party OCR. No contemporary meeting minute, signed stop order, course register or page image was obtained. Soedarmanto p.106 was identified through a nearby footnote but not directly inspected, and that note’s scope is unclear; the cited book is not counted as independent confirmation.
next_verification: Inspect Soedarmanto p.106 and surrounding pages; establish whether it supports the closure account, identify informant/document, then locate Dewanto meeting minutes, order recipients and dated closing/attendance records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Ambarwulan and Kasdi interpret a banner displayed at the 26 September training closure reading “Tunggu Apa Lagi” (“What are you waiting for?”) as a signal that the PKI was ready to begin a rebellion.
claim_type: Retrospective interpretation of an attributed sign/banner
confidence: High that the chapter makes this interpretation; low that the banner existed as reported or conveyed that meaning, because no photograph, contemporary report, witness deposition or organizational instruction was inspected.
basis_and_limitations: The banner and its interpretation appear in the same retrospective narrative; no separate source note for the banner/meaning is visible in the examined passage. Treating the phrase as an operational signal is the authors’ inference, not evidence of a PKI order, shared understanding or planned start date.
next_verification: Find the cited biography passage and its source trail; seek original photographs/film, Air Force information-service logs, contemporaneous press, witnesses and PKI/AURI instructions. Compare whether the phrase was a camp slogan, ceremony banner, or later recollection.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill reports interviews with more than fifty Indonesian exiles in seven countries and seven returnees; the primary materials he used were in Indonesian, and he states that he has no facility in Chinese.
period: Research published 2020; interview base dates mainly 2007–2012
confidence: High that the article states this methodology; it does not independently validate each interview claim.
basis_and_limitations: Hill, printed pp.338–340 and note 1. Interviews are retrospective, and some requested anonymity; IISH archival documents are cited but not all directly reproduced.
next_verification: Inspect the article's interview appendix if available, locate cited IISH papers and recordings, and compare Chinese-language records through qualified translations.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill identifies PKI Politburo/Central Committee member Jusuf Adjitorop as born Josef Simanjuntak, sent to China for medical treatment on 26 June 1964, and later known by the name adopted for underground organizing in North Sumatra; Hill reports a birth-date discrepancy between 19 December 1918 and the later 20 June 1920 date used on a school certificate.
claim_type: Biographical account based on participant papers and secondary scholarship
confidence: High that Hill reports these facts and the date discrepancy; moderate for the underlying biographical particulars pending direct inspection of the autobiography and civil/school records.
basis_and_limitations: Hill, printed pp.349–350 and note 30; he says the biography relies primarily on Adjitorop's 12-page autobiography in IISH Bundle IV, Item 23, which was not directly read here.
next_verification: Obtain IISH Bundle IV, Item 23; compare school certificate, party biography, medical/travel documentation and Indonesian identity records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill quotes Adjitorop's autobiography as saying that on 22 February 1966 he received a Politburo decision authorizing him to lead the PKI Central Committee Delegation abroad.
claim_type: Retrospective autobiographical statement transmitted by scholarship
confidence: High that Hill reports this statement; moderate-to-low that the quoted decision occurred in precisely this form until the cited paper is inspected.
basis_and_limitations: Hill, printed p.350, note 31 cites Jusuf Adjitorop Papers, Indonesian Exiles of the Left collection, IISH, Bundle IV, Item 23, p.12; the original is not directly inspected.
next_verification: Retrieve the autobiography, any written Politburo decision, Delegation appointment notice, and early 1966 communications to party branches.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill reports that Beijing recognized the CC-PKI Delegation as the sole legitimate representation of the PKI abroad; it sent representatives to sympathetic countries and authorized overseas publications, giving it a role in external representation and exile communications.
confidence: High that Hill describes these functions; moderate for the underlying institutional arrangements because the cited evidence is mainly exile interviews and secondary scholarship.
basis_and_limitations: Hill, printed pp.352–353 and notes 34–39. Recognition and overseas representation do not establish that the Delegation commanded domestic Emergency CC, Kompro cells, or operations inside Indonesia.
next_verification: Locate Delegation appointment/authorization papers, publication mastheads and correspondence with Albania, Vietnam and other branches; compare home-party messages and host-state records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill reports that a 7 August 1966 declaration attributed to the PKI Politburo called for a united front under PKI leadership and development of armed struggle against the Suharto–Nasution regime.
claim_type: Published political declaration reported through secondary citations
confidence: High that Hill reports this wording and political program; moderate-to-low for the declaration's exact authorship, circulation and relation to domestic operations.
basis_and_limitations: Hill, printed p.353, cites Simon 1969, pp.173–174, via Sukma 1999, p.50. The original declaration was not opened. It is an exile political program, not proof that a domestic armed operation was authorized or implemented.
next_verification: Find the original declaration, date-stamped copies, publication issue, recipient lists and any home-branch response.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill reports that around a year after the September 1965 upheaval the Beijing Delegation published a new PKI program known as the Auto-criticism, but his supporting references are secondary publications and a 2000 reprint rather than the original publication inspected in this pass.
confidence: High that Hill reports the publication; moderate for exact publication date, edition and circulation.
basis_and_limitations: Hill, printed p.353, note 37 cites van der Kroef 1970 and Sudisman 2000, pp.81–139. This publication claim must be kept separate from the September 1966 Politburo self-criticism written by surviving leaders inside Indonesia.
next_verification: Compare overseas publication scans, Sudisman 2000 reprint, original Indonesian manuscript and correspondence about editorial changes.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill's exile-history reconstruction says the Chinese Communist Party, as host, determined key conditions such as where Indonesian exiles lived and worked and what funding they received; contact with Chinese authorities was conducted primarily, perhaps exclusively, through the Delegation.
confidence: High that Hill makes this account; moderate for the arrangements as reported, pending Chinese and Indonesian administrative records.
basis_and_limitations: Hill, printed pp.354–359, drawing on exile interviews and memoirs. It concerns the living and political conditions of exiles after 1965; it is not evidence of Chinese direction of G30S, arms delivery for the September operation, or command over domestic PKI networks.
next_verification: Seek Chinese Foreign Ministry/CCP liaison, residence, work-assignment and funding records; compare named exile testimony and Delegation correspondence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill documents internal opposition to Adjitorop's call for cadres abroad to regroup in China and a 1968 attempt by the BPKK, chaired by Tom Iljas with A.S. Munandar as deputy, to convene a cadres' conference; Hill says the attempt failed after most Delegation members withdrew support and Chinese authorities denied venue or infrastructure access without Delegation authorization.
claim_type: Exile organizational history from retrospective interviews and memoirs
confidence: High that Hill reports the dispute and failed conference attempt; moderate for exact motives and decision procedure absent minutes or host-government papers.
basis_and_limitations: Hill, printed pp.356–358 and notes 48–53. One opposition group was called Cingkan Syang; Hill cites exile memoirs/interviews. The conflict describes a party-in-exile and must not be collapsed into domestic PKI leadership debates.
next_verification: Find BPKK proposals/minutes, conference invitations and venue requests, Delegation replies, host correspondence, and interviews from participants on opposing sides.

atomic_claim_or_observation: An unsigned April 1978 political document cited by Hill says the overseas CC-PKI Delegation was part of the PKI Central Committee at home and could not replace it; Hill assesses that it had no effective communication with the domestic Central Committee destroyed by the New Order.
claim_type: Unsigned internal political document and scholarly interpretation
confidence: High that Hill reports the document and his interpretation; moderate that the document accurately states the Delegation's internal mandate; low for the exact extent of contact without correspondence.
basis_and_limitations: Hill, printed p.366, note 74 cites an unsigned 20-page document in IISH, Adjitorop Papers, Item 49, p.20; the document was not directly read. Hill's domestic emergency-committee detail in note 75 expressly cites Hearman 2010a, so it is derivative of S1310 rather than independent corroboration.
next_verification: Retrieve IISH Item 49 and any transmission logs; compare with domestic Central Committee and South Blitar records, surviving couriers and correspondence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Academic citations to the Omar Dani Mahmilub case identify different transcript configurations: Oey Hong Lee cites Vol. II, pp.131 and 140, while van der Kroef cites book I, pp.3, 287 and 320 for the 23 December 1966 case file; these references cannot yet be reconciled.
confidence: High for what the two articles cite; no conclusion about whether these are separate editions, transcript sections, or a multi-book set.
basis_and_limitations: Oey also notes name spellings Dani/Dhani; van der Kroef says Oejeng Soewargana supplied the mimeographed transcripts. Neither author citation gives us the underlying pages.
next_verification: Locate and inspect the cited copies, title pages, volume statements, pagination, table of contents and file provenance; compare with Cornell and Mahkamah Agung holdings.

atomic_claim_or_observation: ANRI's Sukarno-era defense/security guide describes KOTI inventory item 63 as a one-folder 1966 copy of the Mahmilub verdict file in the Omar Dani case; this is a judgment-file finding aid, not evidence that ANRI holds the multi-volume trial transcript cited by scholars.
confidence: High for the guide's item description; no confidence assigned to the unseen file contents.
basis_and_limitations: ANRI guide, KOTI item 63, directly rechecked. Item title and folder count locate the file only; its contents were not opened.
next_verification: Request the folder, confirm file title/page count and whether judgment, attachments, hearing minutes or transcript copies are present; then search separate transcript holdings.

atomic_claim_or_observation: ANRI's 1966–1967 photo inventory places the Mahmilub proceedings against former Air Force commander Omar Dhani at Bappenas in Jakarta from 5 to 24 December 1966 and lists individual courtroom photographs; one caption uses the name form “Omar Said,” which should not be silently normalized to Omar Dani/Dhani.
claim_type: Official photographic finding aid and caption metadata
confidence: High for the inventory's dates, captions and item numbers; no claim about what the photographs prove.
basis_and_limitations: ANRI photo inventory printed p.555; items 4679, 4680 and adjacent captions refer to Omar Dhani and the presiding judge; item 4689 says “Men/Pangau Omar Said.” Negatives and prints were not inspected.
next_verification: Request photo items/negatives and verify each caption against the image, trial chronology, court roster and contemporary reporting.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A 2003 Hukumonline table gives Omar Dani's Mahmilub judgment number as PTS-017/MLB/XIV/OD/1966, dated 23 December 1966, and states that its list of tried figures comes from the 1994 State Secretariat history.
confidence: High that the article prints the number/date and identifies its source; the original judgment and the 1994 book were not inspected here.
basis_and_limitations: Hukumonline's table is a secondary transcription of a 1994 state-history list, with possible copying or typographical errors; it is not a primary court record.
next_verification: Obtain the judgment, docket and 1994 history pages and compare the case number, date, spelling, offense, sentence and source note.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Presidential Instruction No. 5/1979 ordered the State Secretary to perfect a White Book on G30S/PKI already prepared by KOPKAMTIB, allowed a cross-agency team, set the task deadline at the end of December 1979, and charged costs to the State Secretariat budget.
claim_type: Primary presidential instruction establishing official narrative-production process
confidence: High for the instruction's wording and institutional procedure; it does not establish the accuracy or exact later edits of the narrative.
basis_and_limitations: Official two-page PDF, clauses 1–4 and preamble. The instruction proves a revision mandate and state funding route, not the historical truth of claims in a resulting white paper.
next_verification: Locate the initial KOPKAMTIB white-book edition, the State Secretariat revised edition and cross-agency drafting files; collate text changes and contributor records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Mardanas Safwan's state-published biography recounts an expanded PKI Politburo meeting on 28 August 1965 and says the meeting delegated full authority to Aidit; its notes cite the 1978 KOPKAMTIB publication G 30 S/PKI, pp.77 and 121.
claim_type: Official military/state narrative with an identified citation chain
confidence: High that the biography makes the claim and names its citation; low-to-moderate that the meeting and delegation occurred exactly as narrated without contemporaneous minutes or direct reading of the cited book.
basis_and_limitations: Safwan, printed pp.67–78; p.59 note cites KOPKAMTIB 1978 p.77, and p.78 note 6 cites p.121. In the account, silence in the meeting is interpreted as full delegation and Aidit is said to set out an operation plan. The 1978 source itself was not read, and the 1979 Inpres shows a later revision process without disclosing its exact edits.
next_verification: Obtain the 1978 KOPKAMTIB book and 1979 revised White Book, compare page-level wording, and seek 28 August attendance, minutes, correspondence and dispatch records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Safwan's attributed 28 August account conflicts with later courtroom accounts: Njono testified that the Politburo did not approve the officers' initiative to act first, while Munir described the briefing as ending without a decision or assent/dissent; the full meeting procedure remains unresolved.
claim_type: Cross-source conflict between defendant testimony and official retrospective narrative
confidence: High that the sources present different accounts; low confidence in selecting one account absent contemporaneous minutes, dispatches and independent participants.
basis_and_limitations: Compare C2400 and C2439 with Safwan pp.72–74. The court statements are later testimony under military prosecution; Safwan's account is state-published and cites KOPKAMTIB. The terms 'briefing', 'expanded Politburo meeting' and later Daily Board decisions may refer to different moments; do not flatten them into a single unanimous decision.
next_verification: Find Politburo attendance lists/minutes, daily-board notes, the alleged letter to Sukarno, courier/radio records, and all attendees' testimony in original transcript form.

atomic_claim_or_observation: In a 23 May 1960 speech excerpt published in New Age, Aidit said the PKI’s lessons from the 1945–48 revolutionary period included combining rural guerrilla struggle, workers’ revolutionary action in occupied towns and work within the opposing armed forces; in the same excerpt he called for consolidating a National Front and building a broad mass party.
confidence: High that the excerpt publicly states this line; low as evidence of 1960s implementation or operational military capacity.
basis_and_limitations: The New Age item identifies itself as an excerpt from the concluding portions of Aidit’s speech. It records the party’s retrospective theory and public program; it does not show what units, training, weapons, orders or actual activity existed in 1960 or 1965.
next_verification: Locate the full Indonesian speech and official PKI publication, compare New Age translation with Indonesian text and the 1966 Political Bureau self-criticism; seek training, liaison and armed-force records to establish implementation.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Aidit’s public 1960 discussion of three forms of struggle coexisted with the PKI line that Lin and Galway characterize for 1950–65 as cross-class cooperation and a nonviolent parliamentary strategy; the difference requires separate examination of doctrine, actual organizational channels and operational capacity.
confidence: Medium: the statements and interpretation are documented, but how doctrine translated into practice varied by period and organizational unit.
basis_and_limitations: Aidit’s 1960 text is a partial public speech excerpt; Lin and Galway’s 2023 argument is an intellectual-history interpretation of leadership writings and speeches. The juxtaposition does not settle whether a policy was militarized, peaceful, or inconsistently applied in every locality; it prevents inferring a standing guerrilla force from strategic language alone.
next_verification: Compare the complete Aidit speech, PKI program and congress decisions, 1966 self-criticism, Fifth Force records, Biro Chusus evidence and provincial training/weapon records in date order.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Ho Hui Ling reports that the CPM Central Committee announced resumption of armed struggle on 1 June 1968 and that the first renewed attack inside Peninsular Malaysia occurred on 17 June near Kroh after crossing from southern Thailand; the article situates this in the 1948–60 Emergency-era war and a continuing cross-border organization.
claim_type: Comparative party chronology reported by secondary scholarship
confidence: Medium-high for the dates as reported in the reviewed literature; primary CPM orders and Malaysian incident records were not read.
basis_and_limitations: Ho Hui Ling’s full article describes the 1 June decision, 17 June ambush and Thai-border base. It is a secondary reconstruction, partly drawing on government white papers and later histories. Do not treat this as evidence about the PKI or equate the CPM’s armed structure with South Blitar.
next_verification: Compare the CPM Central Committee declaration, Malaysia’s 1968 white paper and police/army incident reports for Kroh; locate Chin Peng/Musa Ahmad records and Thai-border camp/recruiting evidence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Ho Hui Ling reports estimates of nearly 800 CPM fighters by 1964, compared with fewer than 300 in 1960, and about 2,047 before the 1968 renewed campaign, including a reported composition across Malaysian and Thai Chinese, Malay, Orang Asli and other recruits.
confidence: Low for the underlying counts and ethnic breakdown; high that the article reports them.
basis_and_limitations: The figures are attributed to Ward and Miraflor (2003) and Mohd Reduan (1993), not to a contemporaneous roster. Definitions of fighter/member/recruit and the counting date are not fully transparent in the excerpt reviewed. Do not use as a directly comparable ratio against PKI party membership, South Blitar cells or U.S. estimates.
next_verification: Find the cited books and their source notes; search CPM regimental lists, Thai and Malaysian security files, demobilization records and individual veteran rolls; retain range and date definitions.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Ho Hui Ling describes CPM external channels through China that reportedly included protection for leaders in Beijing, training, a radio station, advice and financial assistance; her account cites Ho (2010), Miller (1972) and Chin Peng’s memoir.
claim_type: Foreign-support mechanism reported by secondary scholarship
confidence: High that the two later studies report CPM channels to China including advice, training, radio facilities and financial assistance; low-to-moderate for exact dates, amounts and executed transfers without underlying records.
basis_and_limitations: Ho Hui Ling’s article cites Ho (2010), Miller (1972) and Chin Peng’s memoir for Beijing protection, training, broadcasting/advice and finance. Ong’s preliminary paper quotes Chin Peng’s memoir about an initial transmitter request, a 1967 assurance from Mao and the 1969 VMR launch, then analyzes VMR transcript material accessed through Singapore ISD. Neither study presents the Chinese authorization or payment ledger here. The reported CPM channel is comparative, not evidence that PRC supplied equivalent support or operational control to the PKI.
next_verification: Inspect Ho 2010, Miller 1972, Chin Peng memoir and relevant Chinese/CPM records for authorization, dates, recipients, broadcasts and actual transfers.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The Malaysian government’s 1971 white paper states that its purpose was to inform the public and strengthen cooperation with the government; it frames the CPM threat as a reason for parallel security measures and economic/social integration, and says its account continues the November 1968 white paper.
confidence: High that the document states this purpose and framing; it is not independent evidence that all CPM accusations are correct.
basis_and_limitations: Foreword and Introduction, printed pp.v–vi and paras.1–2. The document directly evidences Malaysian government public messaging and its stated strategy; it has an explicit security-mobilization purpose and should be compared with CPM primary documents and neutral/independent records.
next_verification: Obtain the original November 1968 White Paper and its production files; compare the 1968 edition with the 1971 reprint and extract which claims were new.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 1971 Malaysian white paper quotes an alleged captured CPM directive instructing small local units of three to five members to organize underground cells; suitable recruits would receive several days’ training and pistols, mines or grenades, with temporary withdrawal to Thai territory considered if an assault unit faced serious danger.
period: Directive quoted in 1971; relates to CPM build-up from 1968
claim_type: Government publication quoting alleged captured operational document
confidence: High that the white paper prints this excerpt; low-to-moderate that the redacted excerpt is complete, authentic and representative without the original document and custody record.
basis_and_limitations: White paper para.21 reproduces a “captured document” and refers to infiltration-group instructions. The original item, translation, capture circumstances and unredacted context are unavailable in the reviewed publication; this is not proof every local cell was armed or trained as directed.
next_verification: Find the captured paper, Malay/Chinese original, seizure inventory, forensic/authentication report, interrogation transcript and evidence of delivery/receipt of weapons.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 1971 Malaysian white paper quotes arrested or surrendered persons describing village contacts who purchased and stored food at home for later collection by CPM units, alongside small-group reconnaissance, propaganda and recruitment.
period: 1968–1971, as described in a 1971 state paper
claim_type: Official report of attributed detainee/surrender accounts
confidence: High that the paper publishes these accounts; low-to-moderate for independent verification of individual cases and their representativeness.
basis_and_limitations: White paper paras.18–20 and 36–38 quote anonymized statements and report food stores, local suppliers, movement intelligence and logistics. Interrogation conditions, dates of statements, full original transcripts and local corroboration were not available; do not generalize to all villages or supporters.
next_verification: Locate the individual statements and trial files, compare with village testimony and household/market records, and identify precise anonymized locations from archive originals.

atomic_claim_or_observation: In his memoir as quoted by Ong, Chin Peng said an earlier effort to obtain Chinese transmitter equipment for a Vietnam-based station was rejected, while after a late-January 1967 meeting with Mao he was told that CPM would receive radio-station facilities.
period: Before 1964–1967; recalled in a memoir published 2003
claim_type: Attributed memoir statement about foreign-support negotiation
confidence: High that Ong quotes the memoir this way; medium-to-low for the underlying meeting, request and authorization pending the cited memoir and Chinese records.
basis_and_limitations: Ong, p.2, quotes Chin Peng, My Side of the Story, pp.442–449. No Chinese meeting record, facilities agreement or transmission-equipment procurement file was consulted. The chronology is a participant’s retrospective account.
next_verification: Read Chin Peng’s cited pages directly; find Chinese Communist Party international liaison, radio engineering, budget, base-access and equipment files and Vietnam-side correspondence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Ong reports that the CPM’s Voice of the Malayan Revolution began broadcasts on 15 November 1969 from a restricted military base in Hunan under the code Project 691, in Malay, Chinese, English and Tamil; he attributes station staffing above 80 to a 2004 Chin Peng interview volume.
confidence: Medium for the date and station details as reported; the project file, facility logs, broadcast recordings and staff list were not directly opened.
basis_and_limitations: Ong, p.2, cites Chin Peng 2003 pp.442–449 for negotiations and Chin & Hack 2004 p.368 for station location/workforce; he says transcript material was accessed through the Singapore Internal Security Department. A separate US$50 billion facilities-cost estimate in this paper is from a website and is explicitly excluded as unverified.
next_verification: Locate VMR original recordings/transcripts, engineering and station logs, Hunan base records, personnel records, budget and procurement files; compare with Malaysian interception logs and the 1971 white paper.

atomic_claim_or_observation: In a 1987 oral-history interview, Marshall Green said the United States provided Indonesia medicines under an arrangement he described as secret but lawful, and that Indonesia sold some it did not need to earn foreign exchange.
period: Late 1965–1966 as recalled in 1987; shipment and resale dates unspecified
claim_type: Retrospective first-person account of medical assistance and resale
confidence: High that Green made this statement; medium for the underlying shipments and resale because the account is retrospective and no transaction records are present.
basis_and_limitations: LOC/ADST Green transcript, digital lines 131–134, after his account of first private contact with Suharto; interview conducted by Robert J. Martens on 12 May 1987. Green gives no product list, shipment date, quantities, invoices, buyer or recipient record. His account does not resolve the separate November 1965 covert commercial-cover and credit dispute in FRUS d170–d181.
next_verification: Find the final medical list, credit/financing plan, invoices, customs/shipping records, Army or state-store receipts, resale accounts and Green’s cited report to Washington; compare Soemantri/Sukendro and Bunnell testimony.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Green recalled that the U.S. Embassy team had no direct count or eyewitness confirmation of the killings when asked for an estimate in early February 1966; he said the 300,000 figure was an average of country-team members’ guesses and later said a range of roughly 50,000–550,000 would have represented the uncertainty better.
period: Estimate made early February 1966; recalled 12 May 1987
claim_type: Retrospective account of how a diplomatic death estimate was generated
confidence: High that Green described this method and uncertainty; the actual worksheets, individual estimates and underlying local reports have not been found, so this does not establish the true death toll.
basis_and_limitations: LOC/ADST Green transcript, digital lines 152–156. Green said reports were vague and that Embassy staff had seen no bodies or met a witness; these are his 1987 recollections, not proof that no better information existed elsewhere in the U.S. government or in Indonesia.
next_verification: Locate Green’s February 1966 briefing cable, country-team estimate worksheets, consular/mission reports and Washington briefing records; compare the estimate’s geographic/time denominator with Indonesian and local victim documentation.

atomic_claim_or_observation: In the 1987 interview Green attributed the PKI’s rapid collapse partly to its mass membership being spread thin, insufficient cadre training and discipline, and inability to withstand a crisis; this is his retrospective diagnosis, not an independently demonstrated causal account.
claim_type: Former U.S. ambassador’s retrospective causal interpretation
confidence: High for what Green said; low for its explanatory weight absent independent PKI membership, training, discipline and branch-level evidence.
basis_and_limitations: LOC/ADST Green transcript, digital lines 140–145. His answer follows an interviewer’s comparison with Chinese revolutionary warfare; it remains a memory-based diagnosis, not a neutral measure of party discipline or branch capability.
next_verification: Compare PKI member/cadre records, training and branch reports, emergency leadership correspondence, provincial party breakdowns, survivor accounts and other contemporary analyses.

atomic_claim_or_observation: In the same interview Green agreed that the PKI’s reliance on Sukarno left it vulnerable after his authority weakened and added that association with the Chinese Communist Party made it more exposed because he viewed Chinese people as unpopular in Indonesia.
claim_type: Former U.S. ambassador’s retrospective political interpretation
confidence: High for the interview content; low for the causal claims until tested against Indonesian public opinion, party records, Indonesian–Chinese community distinctions and regional evidence.
basis_and_limitations: LOC/ADST Green transcript, digital lines 146–147. The reliance-on-Sukarno proposition was introduced by interviewer Martens and endorsed by Green; Green added the CCP association explanation. Do not collapse the PRC government, ethnic Chinese Indonesians and PKI into a single group.
next_verification: Find PKI/Sukarno correspondence and public statements; regional evidence on attitudes to China and Chinese Indonesians; compare membership, repression and survival patterns across regions.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Green recalled that roughly eleven or twelve Army battalions he described as pro-communist were sent to outer islands and “never heard of again”; he named no units, dates, destinations, orders or personnel outcomes.
confidence: High that Green made this statement; low for the number, unit identity, movement, motive or subsequent fate because no operational records or unit names are supplied.
basis_and_limitations: LOC/ADST Green transcript, digital lines 203–205. This is an undated recollection by a U.S. ambassador; the label “pro-communist” is Green’s and requires unit-specific verification. FRUS d176 (S470) separately reports one brigade returned from the Malaysia confrontation theater to Central/East Java in Nov 1965; it does not identify the units or corroborate Green’s 11–12 battalions-to-outer-islands recollection. This is a distinct movement lead, not confirmation of the same claim.
next_verification: Identify battalions transferred to outer-island commands in late 1965–1966; seek movement orders, rosters, relief/replacement records, command histories and family/personnel tracing. Compare separately with the one-brigade Central/East Java redeployment in S470.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A U.S. Embassy cover report dated 28 February 1968 says it received a translated 17 February report from Indonesian Army General Staff I/SUAD-I, based on captured documents and interrogation of PKI captives, via businessman and political activist Husein Ahmaduddin, who had contacts in SUAD-I.
confidence: High that the Embassy record describes this provenance and transmission; the underlying interrogation and captured documents were not accessed.
basis_and_limitations: Embassy cover note at PDF/OCR lines 14–16; the cover identifies Ahmaduddin as intermediary and attributes the enclosure to SUAD-I. It does not provide the original TNI file, source identities or interrogation protocol.
next_verification: Obtain the original SUAD-I file and distribution log, Ahmaduddin’s transmission context, captured-document inventory, and the interrogation records and conditions.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The translated TNI report attributes to captive Subandi the statement that the South Blitar KOMPRO was headed by Tarmudji, described as a former East Java CDB member; it assigns Subandi to supplies/logistics, Ucup to PP, Parto to GRMAS, Suwarno to the armed-struggle section, and Sono to BAGITROP.
claim_type: Captured-person testimony reproduced in military intelligence report
confidence: High that the report makes these attributions; low-to-moderate for exact identity, authority and actual duties without independent rosters or party records.
basis_and_limitations: S1487, enclosure section III, PDF/OCR lines 124–145. The report inconsistently spells the section as PERDJUTA/PERMUTA and the subsection as GRMAS/GERMAS; aliases and real-name key are unavailable.
next_verification: Find Tarmudji, Subandi and Ucup/Parto/Sono/Suwarno identity keys, Kompro rosters, captured papers, local trial files and independent East Java CDB accounts.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The 17 February TNI report describes East Java Kompro and city-trio structures under the slogan “villages surround the cities,” with three organizational, armed-struggle, and agitation/propaganda sections; it lists multiple mountain-region Kompro and says a Wilis-area unit is only suspected.
claim_type: Contemporaneous military intelligence description of clandestine organization
confidence: High that the report presents this structure; low-to-moderate for how broadly or consistently it existed because the report relies on captives and captured documents and gives no complete rosters or execution records.
basis_and_limitations: S1487, enclosure sections I–II and IV, PDF/OCR lines 57–123, 168–194. Distinguish the report’s asserted organizational map from independently confirmed operational capacity.
next_verification: Find region-by-region membership, courier, meeting, finance, and training records; compare captured documents with Rewang, Liem, Hearman and provincial trials.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The TNI report says a planned general conflict for early 1968 did not begin because concrete readiness reports from other regions were absent; Rewang later recalled that no start date had been set and that an armed campaign required approval by a meeting of provincial committees. The decision chronology is unresolved.
claim_type: Conflict between interrogation-based military intelligence and retrospective participant testimony
confidence: High that the two sources make these different claims; neither establishes a single nationwide order or actual launch date.
basis_and_limitations: S1487, enclosure section IV(4)(a), PDF/OCR lines 184–187; Hearman, “Guerrillas, Guns, and Knives?”, printed pp.80–81 and note 104, based on her Rewang interview; Liem’s 2004 interview-based account is separately registered in S1317. The TNI report is a translated account based on captives/captured papers; Rewang’s statements are later participant recollections. No minutes, regional readiness reports or original captured papers resolve whether the sources describe different stages or conflict.
next_verification: Locate the cited captured documents, any national conference agenda/minutes, regional readiness reports, emergency-committee instructions and Rewang’s original interview recording.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The TNI report attributes to captive-derived material a split between a Sudisman bloc described as Maoist and a Sakirman bloc labeled “Modern Revisionist”; no PKI factional minutes or correspondence confirming this formulation were obtained.
claim_type: Interrogation-derived account of alleged internal political divisions
confidence: High that this wording appears in the report; low for the faction labels, boundaries and consequences as an accurate party-wide map.
basis_and_limitations: S1487, enclosure section III, PDF/OCR lines 168–170. These are the Army report’s labels, not neutral or independently verified names for stable organized factions.
next_verification: Compare Sudisman, Sakirman, Ismail Bakri and Rewang correspondence, trial defenses, party documents, and separate participant interviews.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The TNI report says captives described PKI political education as condemning the earlier military-commissar approach because officers cultivated by the party had instead exploited the party during the September 30 Movement; this is a reported post-defeat diagnosis, not proof of the earlier system’s full operation.
period: 1965 and retrospective account in 1968; East Java
claim_type: Captured-person account of PKI internal criticism of military-political relations
confidence: High that the report reproduces this criticism; moderate-to-low that it accurately reflects a collective party decision or the actual reach of the earlier commissar system.
basis_and_limitations: S1487, enclosure section IV(4)(f), PDF/OCR lines 188–194; the report does not attach the cited curriculum, meeting minutes or military-cultivation roster.
next_verification: Compare with 1966 PKI self-criticism, Fifth Force/armed-forces advisory proposals, Biro Chusus papers, officer recruitment lists and regional military records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The U.S. Embassy cover report says it lacked collateral information to confirm that the reported Blitar “revenge killings” were committed by a cohesive PKI group; it notes local religious/social tension and undisciplined, underpaid soldiers involved in robbery as alternative explanations.
claim_type: Contemporaneous U.S. Embassy assessment explicitly limiting attribution
confidence: High that the Embassy made this caveat; it does not identify the actual perpetrators of any specific killing.
basis_and_limitations: S1487, Embassy cover report, PDF/OCR lines 27–41. The Embassy’s alternatives are analytical possibilities, not established alternative perpetrators; distinguish these caveats from the TNI enclosure’s allegations.
next_verification: Identify each killing by date, location, victim, witness, arrest file and unit; compare local police, military, village, family and court records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The TNI report recommended intensified territorial/intelligence work, special combat troops because local forces were said to be insufficient, tighter firearms/ammunition controls and improved ordinary-soldier welfare; these are recommendations, not proof the measures were implemented.
claim_type: Indonesian Army General Staff operational recommendation
confidence: High for the recommendations printed in the translated report; implementation and the underlying assessment of local units remain unverified.
basis_and_limitations: S1487, enclosure section VI, PDF/OCR lines 211–219. The report is an Embassy translation; no signed implementation order or follow-up log is attached.
next_verification: Find Kodam VIII/Brawijaya operational orders, unit deployments, arms-control directives, welfare/pay records and subsequent situation reports.

atomic_claim_or_observation: ANRI’s diplomatic-archives guide lists Sukarno’s opening address to KIAPMA at Hotel Indonesia on 17 October 1965 as one stencilled sheet, inventory No.817.
confidence: High that the finding aid contains this entry; it does not establish access to or full content of the underlying speech.
basis_and_limitations: Official guide, printed p.31, item 234.
next_verification: Retrieve and inspect ANRI record No.817 and its file cover.

atomic_claim_or_observation: ANRI’s virtual exhibition caption attributes an English-language one-page typescript for Sukarno’s KIAPMA opening address to inventory No.817; the official inventory instead describes No.817 as a one-sheet Indonesian-language stencilled text. The relation between the two witnesses is unresolved.
confidence: High that the gallery image and catalogue entry differ in language/description; low for whether the image is a translation, alternate copy or mismapped item.
basis_and_limitations: Visual gallery inspection; ANRI guide p.31/item 234. Do not treat the English image as the original or complete transcript.
next_verification: Request underlying No.817, provenance of gallery scan, Cabinet Secretariat number 1181/65 and any English translation file.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The Dutch National Archives finding aid describes a physical folder on KIAPMA in Jakarta dated 17–21 October 1965.
confidence: High that the finding aid gives this folder title and span; no conference act or diplomatic view can be inferred from the title.
basis_and_limitations: Archive 2.05.188, printed p.58, item 761; folder contents not opened.
next_verification: Request item 761 and identify its creator, enclosures and actual dates.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Peking Review reported KIAPMA took place 17–20 October 1965 and had more than 200 delegates from 55 countries/regions and four international organizations.
claim_type: Contemporary published report and attendance estimate
confidence: High that the periodical reports these dates and numbers; moderate-to-low for attendance count because no roll or independent count was found.
basis_and_limitations: Peking Review No.45, pp.16–18; ideological report.
next_verification: Locate attendance lists, proceedings, invitations and independent Indonesian/foreign press coverage.

atomic_claim_or_observation: World Outlook quoted Le Figaro correspondent J. Jacquet-Francillon reporting 160 delegates representing 54 nations at KIAPMA.
claim_type: Contemporary press report quoted by a later outlet
confidence: High that World Outlook prints this attribution; low-to-moderate for the count and its comparability with Peking Review because the original Le Figaro issue and counting definitions are missing.
basis_and_limitations: World Outlook No.31, pp.6–7; its quotation is a mediated report, not an independent second count.
next_verification: Retrieve the original Le Figaro dispatch and compare registered delegates, organizations, observers and countries/regions.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Peking Review reported military and armoured security around KIAPMA, a curfew and restrictions on delegates’ telephone/telegraph access, and arrests of Indonesian conference workers.
confidence: High that the publications made these reports; moderate-to-low for their scope and details until rosters, police/military records and independent delegate accounts are checked.
basis_and_limitations: Peking Review No.45 pp.16–18; Alley is a participant account with strong political framing; World Outlook quotes Le Figaro.
next_verification: Find conference staff lists, arrest/detention files, hotel logs, press restrictions and independent participants’ notes.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Peking Review reported that Indonesian troops searched the Chinese Commercial Counsellor’s Office on 16 October and that China’s delegation protested; it said delegation head Tang Ming-chao did not attend Sukarno’s opening.
claim_type: Foreign-government allegation and reported diplomatic reaction
confidence: High that PRC publication and Reuters issue preview report the allegation/protest; the precise object searched and the reason for the delegation head’s absence are not independently established.
basis_and_limitations: Peking Review No.45 p.17; Straits Times Reuters preview says China protested an alleged search.
next_verification: Obtain Chinese diplomatic protest, Army unit records, Indonesian MFA property register and conference attendance record.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Peking Review No.46 quoted an Army Strategic Reserve Command statement acknowledging that a 328th Battalion unit entered and searched the Commercial Counsellor’s Office on 16 October, while saying that nothing improper was found.
claim_type: Military statement quoted in a foreign publication
confidence: High that the PRC publication reproduces this attributed statement; moderate for the exact statement until the original Army release is found.
basis_and_limitations: Peking Review No.46; the Army release itself was not retrieved.
next_verification: Locate the Army press statement, its original Indonesian wording, issuing authority and any search/property record.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Peking Review No.46 reproduced an Indonesian Foreign Ministry note dated 30 October reporting that military administrator Umar Wirahadikusumah apologized to Sukarno on 28 October over the 16 October search and promised no repeat.
claim_type: Diplomatic report quoted by foreign publication
confidence: High that the periodical reports this note and apology; moderate-to-low for exact wording and scope without the note itself.
basis_and_limitations: This is the note as reproduced in a PRC party-state publication; the Indonesian original, delivery registry and diplomatic-property register were not obtained.
next_verification: Retrieve the original Foreign Ministry note, its delivery registry, Chinese response and Indonesian property/protocol records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Arthur J. Dommen’s 1966 article states that the Chinese Commercial Counsellor’s house and office were not officially listed as Embassy property at the Indonesian Foreign Ministry.
claim_type: Contemporaneous scholarly assertion about diplomatic property registration
confidence: High that Dommen makes the footnote assertion; low-to-moderate for the underlying legal fact until the register and relevant Vienna-era diplomatic status rules are checked.
basis_and_limitations: Dommen, note 16; full article text and Ministry register not reviewed. The statement does not itself settle immunity or legality.
next_verification: Locate Indonesian MFA diplomatic-property/protocol register and the relevant note verbales and site designations.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Rewi Alley’s December 1965 essay says he was in Jakarta from 13–23 October to attend KIAPMA and describes raids, arrests and restrictions he says he witnessed or learned about.
confidence: High that the hosted text makes these statements; moderate for attendance, lower for specific events without identifying which were personally observed and independent corroboration.
basis_and_limitations: Transcription of The People’s Voice; strong anti-imperialist and pro-PKI framing; original print issue not obtained.
next_verification: Locate original issue, named co-delegates, diaries and police/arrest records; separate firsthand observation from hearsay.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Taomo Zhou reports AAJA was established in Jakarta in 1963 after a conference attended by journalists from 47 countries, and later had a Jakarta office and publication/training activities.
confidence: High that the study reports these organizational features; moderate-high pending original statutes, membership lists and issues.
basis_and_limitations: Peer-reviewed article; trace its references to AAJA publications and records.
next_verification: Obtain the 1963 Jakarta Declaration, founding meeting record, membership register and early Afro-Asian Journalist issues.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Zhou reports that the Indonesian Army searched the Jakarta AAJA headquarters in December 1965, confiscated documents, cut external communications and arrested three people.
claim_type: Scholarly account of repression of a transnational press organization
confidence: High that the article reports this sequence; moderate for occurrence and individual identities because cited support includes an AAJA publication and a later interview.
basis_and_limitations: Zhou cites Afro-Asian Journalist 1966a p.39 and interview with Liz Morrison; no Indonesian search inventory/arrest file retrieved.
next_verification: Find the AAJA magazine article, Indonesian police/military files, office lease and arrest/detention records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: An AAJA cable reproduced in a 15 January 1966 U.S. Embassy file protested the Indonesian Armed Forces’ arrest of Joesoef, identified in the cable as the Association’s acting secretary-general.
claim_type: Archival record of an organization’s protest
confidence: High that the cable and allegation appear in the Embassy file; the cable alone does not independently establish the circumstances or legal basis of arrest.
basis_and_limitations: NARA RG84 Entry P339 Box24 scan, first page; OCR/name spelling uncertain.
next_verification: Find the arrest warrant, detainee registry, court file, original AAJA cable and Joesoef’s full identity record.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The AAJA representatives’ 15 January press-conference statement said direct calls and letters from Jakarta had not reached the secretariat and the office telephone was disconnected; it announced a temporary withdrawal of the secretariat from Jakarta.
claim_type: Organizational statement recorded in a U.S. diplomatic file
confidence: High that the statement reports these conditions and a temporary withdrawal; moderate for communication failure and its duration pending carrier/telegraph logs.
basis_and_limitations: NARA RG84 scan pp.1–3; noisy OCR. Statement is interested testimony.
next_verification: Locate telephone/telegraph service records, AAJA minutes, correspondence and exact December departure date.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The same press-conference account said the All-China Journalists’ Association offered temporary premises/facilities to the AAJA secretariat in Beijing.
confidence: High that AAJA publicly reported this offer; this proves the stated offer, not how long the facilities were supplied or the degree of PRC control.
basis_and_limitations: NARA file is an Embassy rendering/report of the conference, not a Chinese association contract or budget.
next_verification: Find All-China Journalists’ Association records, space/funding agreements and later AAJA office administration files.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The AAJA fourth enlarged Secretariat plenary met in Beijing on 20–24 April 1966; its published communiqué says it supported temporary withdrawal from Jakarta and kept the Secretariat’s working seat in Beijing until the next conference.
claim_type: Formal communiqué published by Xinhua/People’s Daily
confidence: High for the dates and decisions reported in the communiqué; moderate for actual implementation beyond what later periodicals report.
basis_and_limitations: People’s Daily, 25 Apr 1966 p.3; Le Monde/AFP independently reports 19 country representatives and Beijing seat.
next_verification: Find meeting minutes, attendance list, motion wording and Algerian 1967 conference file.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Le Monde’s AFP report said the April 1966 AAJA plenary adopted anti-U.S./Vietnam and anti-Indonesian-regime resolutions but adopted no anti-revisionist text despite efforts by Chinese delegates.
claim_type: Contemporary news-agency report about conference debate
confidence: High that AFP/Le Monde reported this; moderate for the internal debate because minutes, amendments and individual votes are unavailable.
basis_and_limitations: Subscription-restricted short report; compare with official communiqué but neither supplies the full debate transcript.
next_verification: Retrieve the draft resolutions, minutes, delegate interventions and correspondence among member organizations.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Djawoto’s 16 April 1966 press statement says he had requested release from his ambassadorial post about two months earlier, received no reply from Jakarta, and then announced on his own initiative that he was no longer ambassador from 6 a.m. that day.
confidence: High that Djawoto publicly said this; moderate for the timing and receipt of his cable until the original transmission and Indonesian response records are found.
basis_and_limitations: Watch65/GerakIngatan English PDF; Peking Review reproduces related statement.
next_verification: Find outgoing cable, Indonesian MFA incoming register, Sukarno recall instruction, status of credentials and passport/citizenship actions.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Djawoto’s statement explicitly presents the claim that the CIA and other imperialists played an important role in Indonesia’s post-October political shift as his “personal conviction.”
claim_type: Contemporaneous political allegation attributed to speaker
confidence: High that he made the allegation and marked it as personal conviction; this is not direct evidence of a CIA operation or specific causal mechanism.
basis_and_limitations: Statement’s politically committed framing; no operation-specific evidence is attached.
next_verification: Test each proposed U.S. channel independently through FRUS/CIA records, Indonesian recipients, payments, instructions and timing.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill reports Ibrahim Isa served as Indonesia’s resident representative at AAPSO in Cairo (1960–1965), led a pro-Sukarno Indonesian delegation to the January 1966 Tricontinental Conference in Havana and joined the Beijing CC-PKI Delegation staff after arriving from Havana.
claim_type: Scholarly biography linking international solidarity and PKI exile organizations
confidence: High that the article reports these posts; moderate-high pending travel, appointment and organizational files.
basis_and_limitations: Hill cites McGregor/Hearman, Manap and Hearman; OISRAA, AAPSO, Tricontinental delegation and CC-PKI role are distinct bodies.
next_verification: Retrieve AAPSO appointment files, Havana delegate list, travel/passport record, OISRAA bulletins and Beijing Delegation roster.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Jusuf Adjitorop’s autobiography, as cited by Hill, says he was sent to China for medical treatment in June 1964 and received a Politburo decision on 22 February 1966 authorizing him to lead the PKI Central Committee Delegation abroad.
claim_type: Later participant autobiography cited in peer-reviewed research
confidence: High that the autobiography as cited gives this account; moderate for its complete institutional authorization because the manuscript/minutes were not directly inspected.
basis_and_limitations: Hill cites IISH Jusuf Adjitorop Papers, Bundle IV, Item 23, pp.12; the archive item is not directly retrieved.
next_verification: Request the IISH item, medical/travel record, original Politburo decision and Delegation roster.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill reports Beijing recognized the CC-PKI Delegation as the sole legitimate PKI representation abroad and that it coordinated exile regrouping, publications and overseas party contacts.
claim_type: Scholarly account of an external political-organizational channel
confidence: High that Hill reports the recognition and activities; moderate for the scope of external authority; it does not establish control over domestic underground cells.
basis_and_limitations: Article combines archival and exile sources; distinguish representation abroad from domestic command.
next_verification: Find Chinese recognition/liaison records, Delegation mandates, publication files and communication with specific Indonesian regional groups.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill reports that the Chinese Communist Party host determined major conditions of Indonesian exiles’ residence, work and funding, while communications with Chinese authorities generally passed through the CC-PKI Delegation.
claim_type: Scholarly interpretation of host-state administration and party gatekeeping
confidence: High that this is the article’s documented interpretation; moderate for consistency across all exiles and years. It supports material/communications leverage but not by itself Chinese control of PKI doctrine or Indonesian operations.
basis_and_limitations: Hill draws on interviews, memoirs and archives and also notes that exiles themselves ran much of their criticism/re-education.
next_verification: Seek Chinese liaison, residence, assignment and funding records alongside exiles who opposed or bypassed the Delegation.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill reports that some exiles and military participants criticized Adjitorop’s call for cadres abroad to regroup in China as a strategic mistake that produced disputes and lacked a clear plan.
confidence: High that the cited participants made this criticism; low-to-moderate as an objective assessment of the strategy because it is retrospective testimony from a divided exile community.
basis_and_limitations: Hill cites Suhario Padmodiwiryo 2005 and interviews; record as factional testimony, not settled consensus.
next_verification: Read Padmodiwiryo pp.205, 214, Cingkan Syang documents, and interviews from Delegation supporters and opponents.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill reports that an exile-organized BPKK attempted for more than six months in 1968 to convene a global cadres’ conference; after the Delegation withdrew support, Chinese authorities denied venues/infrastructure and recognized communications only when authorized by Adjitorop’s Delegation, so no conference occurred.
claim_type: Scholarly account of intra-exile dispute and host-state access mechanism
confidence: High that the article reports this sequence; moderate pending the meeting request, host decision and correspondence.
basis_and_limitations: Based on named exile interviews; it shows a reported effect on exile politics, not Chinese control over domestic PKI leadership.
next_verification: Find BPKK invitations/minutes, venue requests, Chinese-host replies and Delegation directives.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Hill cites a later CPM history to report that several hundred Malayan Communist Party cadres completed political and military training at Nanjing Military Academy in the early 1960s; Hill separately says the identity of the Indonesian exile compound as that academy is inferred, not named by his interviewees.
claim_type: Secondary comparative lead about a Southeast Asian communist party
confidence: High that Hill reports this comparison; moderate-to-low for the underlying number and facility identification until CPM/Chinese records are checked. It does not prove the PKI exiles received equivalent military training.
basis_and_limitations: Hill cites Chin 2004 for CPM trainees and Zhou 2014 for the academy identification.
next_verification: Check Chin’s cited page, CPM participant records, Nanjing Academy archives and separate Indonesian exile training accounts.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A Chinese Foreign Ministry note reproduced in Peking Review says China had sent more than 8,200 tons of equipment/materials for the Banjaran mill, exceeding 70% of the total, and had dispatched construction experts.
claim_type: PRC government statement about economic aid
confidence: High that the Ministry’s published note makes these claims; moderate for the quantities pending contracts, shipping/customs records and Indonesian receipts.
basis_and_limitations: The 18 Apr 1966 note is reproduced in a PRC publication; not independently verified in this pass.
next_verification: Locate 1961 cooperation agreement, credit and equipment schedules, shipment manifests, port records and Indonesian plant inventories.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The same Chinese Foreign Ministry note says China stopped its assistance to the Banjaran mill and withdrew its experts after the 15 April 1966 attack on its Jakarta Embassy.
claim_type: PRC government statement on aid suspension and its stated reason
confidence: High that the note declares suspension and withdrawal; moderate for the completion/withdrawal timeline and the causal explanation as a sole cause.
basis_and_limitations: A unilateral diplomatic statement; no bilateral response or personnel departure/shipping logs retrieved.
next_verification: Find expert rosters, project progress reports, shipment contracts, Indonesian/Chinese minutes and later restart decisions.

atomic_claim_or_observation: A 1991 JICA technical study reports Banjaran First Mill construction began in 1965, financed partly with Japanese reparations but mainly with Chinese financial aid; operations began at 30,000 spindles in 1967 and full-scale operation in 1968.
claim_type: Later technical survey and retrospective industrial history
confidence: High that the JICA report states this and documents a 1991 field survey; moderate-high for the mill timeline pending commissioning logs and Indonesian company records.
basis_and_limitations: JICA field team surveyed the plant in 1991; later full operation followed the 1966 Chinese announcement of aid suspension and requires an intervening project history.
next_verification: Find PT Industri Sandang I board minutes, commissioning records, Japanese reparations accounting and resumed Chinese/Indonesian supply records.

atomic_claim_or_observation: JICA’s 1991 field report lists Chinese-made 1964–65 machinery still in Banjaran First Mill equipment and reports production in 1989–90 using mainly Chinese-made machinery.
confidence: High that the survey reports these machines and production; moderate for precise provenance until equipment serials and plant inventories are checked.
basis_and_limitations: A field observation 26 years later supports delivery/use continuity, not the exact 1965 shipment quantities or 1966 aid mechanism.
next_verification: Retrieve machinery inventory, serial plates, Chinese supplier records and post-1966 maintenance/replacement logs.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The September 1966 Political Bureau self-criticism reprinted by the PKI Delegation in 1971 says the leadership committed “adventurism” by violating party organization principles and involving itself in the September 30 Movement without high mass consciousness, thereby isolating the Party from the masses.
period: 1966-09 retrospective account of 1965; Central Java / national party
claim_type: PKI Political Bureau self-criticism as republished by the exile Delegation
confidence: High that the text makes this internal accusation; low-to-moderate as a complete factual description of G30S decision-making because it is retrospective, factional and not supported here by underlying minutes.
basis_and_limitations: 1971 compilation reproduces a text dated Central Java, September 1966; it frames the account within a post-defeat Maoist line.
next_verification: Compare with the August 1966 statement, Supardjo postmortem, Sjam/Untung/Aidit records, party minutes and regional command evidence.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The September 1966 self-criticism says that after the September 30 Movement’s defeat the Party leadership adopted “Right opportunism” by entrusting the fate of the Party and revolutionary movement to President Sukarno’s policy.
confidence: High that the text makes this diagnosis; it is not an independently tested explanation of all PKI decisions or Sukarno’s actual capacity.
basis_and_limitations: Text printed in the Delegation’s 1971 compilation, original 1966 text not directly inspected.
next_verification: Compare Sukarno–Aidit correspondence, Politburo instructions, public appeals, military orders and surviving regional reports.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The September 1966 self-criticism interprets the PKI’s earlier goal of achieving people’s democracy through parliamentary elections/peaceful means as a Rightist deviation, and its later political programme calls for armed peasant struggle and rural revolutionary bases.
claim_type: PKI post-defeat party line and political self-interpretation
confidence: High that the compilation’s texts present this diagnosis and future programme; low as proof that pre-1965 practice was simply peaceful or that the new programme was implemented nationwide.
basis_and_limitations: The compilation is a factional 1971 presentation; doctrinal self-description must be compared with pre-1965 party speeches, organizational practice and regional military evidence.
next_verification: Compare complete 1954/1959/1962/1965 resolutions, Aidit’s 1960 speech, volunteer training, Biro Chusus records and post-1966 domestic underground evidence.

next_verification: Compare the cited Aceh military chronology, Baperki documents, local government reports and independent survivor/family accounts.

next_verification: Find Djuarsa’s signed directive, checkpoint/pass lists, convoy records, port/ship manifests, refugee registration and family/community lists.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Pauker’s 1969 RAND report says Rewang was killed during the 1968 South Blitar campaign; Hearman’s interview-based biography and 1990–91 TAPOL and Amnesty reports identify the same leader as arrested in 1968, tried and imprisoned, then released on 24 July 1991. basis_and_limitations: Pauker printed p.62 says Rewang was killed. Hearman (2010) reports an interview with Rewang on 14 Feb 2009 and a 1971 life sentence; TAPOL 1990 records trial/appeal/commutation and continued detention; TAPOL 1991 and Amnesty confirm the 1991 release. No original trial judgment or prison register has yet been obtained. This establishes a specific report error, not that every RAND estimate is false.
next_verification: Obtain Rewang’s Semarang trial docket and judgment, 1975 appeal, 1985 commutation, Cipinang intake/release registers, family correspondence and the Brawijaya capture log; resolve the 13/14/20/21 July date variants.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The South Blitar “2,000” figure does not have one stable category: Pauker says about 2,000 underground PKI members/leaders were killed; Hearman 2010/2018 and the derivative 1969 press account describe captured-or-killed/arrested totals; Hearman 2017 states 2,000 killed plus thousands detained/displaced. confidence: High for the differences in wording across the sources read; low for a reconciled number or death count.
basis_and_limitations: Pauker p.62 cites NYT July 12 and October 29, 1968 but supplies no method. Hearman 2017 cites NYT 11 Aug 1968 for “2,000 killed”; her other accounts use captured/killed categories. Evans (3 Mar 1969) says the October Times report gave 2,000 killed or captured and a mid-February Times follow-up cut the figure in half. The same author’s later accounts and the derivative reports are not independent counts. The 2010 footnote’s 13 Feb 1968 year is likely anomalous, not yet corrected.
next_verification: Acquire the NYT July 12, Aug 11, Oct 29 1968 and mid-February follow-up through TimesMachine/ProQuest/microfilm; inspect army briefings and Trisula casualty, detention, court, displacement and village records; tabulate each person and outcome once.

basis_and_limitations: The article distinguishes reported TNI numbers, oral histories and later Army narrative. These figures are deployment estimates, not a verified unit muster. Forced work, crop removal, evacuation and detention are distinct from combatant deaths and cannot be folded into casualty totals.
next_verification: Obtain six-battalion operational orders, muster/payroll and militia rolls, village caretaker and screening registers, evacuation/camp lists, food supply records, patrol tasking, road work records, and family interviews from each operation zone.

confidence: High for the estimate’s text and its documented interagency disagreement; lower for the intelligence judgments about actual Chinese transfers and insurgent capacity.
basis_and_limitations: SNIE 51-68 assesses Chinese support as an intelligence estimate, not a receipt record. It is useful alongside the January 1968 CPB offensive and other Southeast Asian party trajectories, but force categories and source quality are not comparable across countries.
next_verification: Compare with CPB and PRC records, local party/ethnic armed-group material, UCDP chronology and later scholarship; distinguish Chinese weapons/training, local insurgent forces, ethnic allies and U.S. estimates.

next_verification: Obtain Pudji Aswati’s arrest/custody chronology, 1978 indictment and judgment, sentence calculation, prison medical file and 1989 release register; seek family and former-prisoner testimony.

next_verification: Locate the court judgment, clemency decision, execution order and civil death record; seek prison correspondence and family-care documentation.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Chandra’s Central Java study uses aggregate population counts from the 1961, 1971, and 1980 censuses, local election returns from 1955 and 1957, and administrative/geographic data to estimate one-time population changes associated with the 1965–66 violence across 29 regencies and six cities.

next_verification: Inspect the article’s table and underlying census tables; compare the estimates with district-level burial, detention, missing-person and refugee records.

confidence: High that the article makes this interpretation; moderate-to-low that census/election correlations alone establish the actual agency or relative responsibility in each locality.
basis_and_limitations: The argument compares 1957 vote shares, estimated population changes, prior local studies and reported RPKAD deployments. The author explicitly cautions that associations and the simplified aliran model cannot establish causality; party support and religious-cultural identification were not identical.
next_verification: Compare original RPKAD movement and operation orders, local Army logs, PNI/NU records, detention lists, trial records and village testimony for each cluster.

atomic_claim_or_observation: The Central Java census reconstruction does not supply a national or regional percentage distribution of victims by ethnicity. Its data are population totals by administrative area plus election/geographic variables, not individual victim identity records; population gaps can also reflect refuge-seeking and other movement.
period: 1965–1966; Central Java and national victim estimates
claim_type: Data-scope finding and limit on ethnic-percentage inference
confidence: High that these sources do not provide a victim-level ethnic distribution; no reliable national victim-level ethnic breakdown was located in this search.
basis_and_limitations: Chandra’s method is ecological and aggregate. Woolgar’s West Java study and Cribb/Coppel address estimates and regional variation in anti-Chinese targeting, but their rounded estimates do not create a national named-victim dataset or an audited ethnic percentage.
next_verification: Seek victim-level records with identity fields from Komnas HAM, YPKP, local cemeteries, detention facilities, civil registration and community archives; assess each region separately and state missingness.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Chandra reports that between the 1955 national and 1957 local elections in Central Java, PKI votes increased by 800,340 while PNI votes fell by 335,944; he calculates a district-level correlation of about −0.53 between changes in their vote shares.

next_verification: Inspect Hindley’s cited table and official election returns; compare local party organization records and contemporary PNI/PKI correspondence.

next_verification: Locate 1951 SOBRI and 1955 Sarbumusi constitutive statutes, regional membership and enterprise elections; do not infer every worker's party affiliation.

confidence: Moderate for reported meeting, arrest and itinerary; primary messenger testimony and arrest register missing; high that author explicitly distinguishes homonyms.

confidence: Moderate for sequence, low-to-moderate for precise participant counts; primary patrol logs and court case files not obtained.

atomic_claim_or_observation: Indonesia's culture ministry encyclopedia reports the 7–8 November 1945 Islamic Congress selected Soekiman as the Masyumi party chair and Abikusno and Wali Al Fatah as deputies, citing 9 November 1945 Kedaulatan Rakyat; this is an attributed later summary and not a complete voter or membership roll.
claim_type: Institutional history citing a contemporaneous press report
